definition: A* searches for a shortest path by expanding the vertex with the smallest f, where f is the distance so far plus a heuristic estimate of the distance remaining. When that estimate never overestimates and is consistent, the first time the goal leaves the frontier the path is optimal. The heuristic is what lets it expand fewer vertices than Dijkstra when a goal is known.
details: An admissible heuristic never overestimates. A consistent heuristic also satisfies the triangle inequality, which keeps the first visit to each vertex optimal.
A heuristic of zero makes A* behave like Dijkstra.

complexity.time: Depends on the heuristic. The worst case is still exponential in the path length; a good heuristic expands far fewer vertices.
complexity.space: O(V) in the worst case for the frontier and the visited set.

examples: Pathfinding on a map, using straight-line distance as the estimate
Route finding in a game grid

definition: An ABI is the binary contract for calling compiled code: how arguments are passed, how values are returned, how the stack is laid out, and how names are encoded. Separately compiled units can be linked only if they share an ABI. It is a binary agreement, distinct from the source-level API.
examples: The calling convention of a system ABI
Two compilers producing code that can call each other

definition: An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated on its own and exists to be extended. It can hold fields and implemented methods, and it can declare methods that subclasses must implement. It sits between a concrete class and a pure interface.
examples: A Shape class with a position field and an abstract area method
A base parser that implements shared bookkeeping and leaves one method abstract

definition: An abstract syntax tree is the tree a parser produces, with a node for each construct and children for its parts. It omits purely syntactic punctuation. Later phases, such as type checking and code generation, walk this tree rather than the source text.
examples: A node for a function call with child nodes for the arguments
A binary node for an addition

definition: Abstraction presents a simpler model of something and hides incidental detail. The caller sees the operations that matter and not the mechanism behind them. A file object offers read and write; the disk layout stays behind that model.
examples: A list interface that does not reveal whether storage is an array or a tree
A payment method that does not expose the processor's protocol

definition: Accounting, in security, is recording who did what, and when, so actions can be reviewed later. It is the third part of authentication, authorization, and accounting. The record is only useful if it is kept where the actor cannot quietly alter it.
prompt: What is accounting in security?
examples: A log of administrative changes with the actor's identity
A record of access to a sensitive record

definition: ACID names the four properties of a reliable transaction: atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. Atomicity makes the group all-or-nothing. Consistency means committed data satisfies the database's constraints. Isolation limits how concurrent transactions see each other. Durability means a committed write survives a crash.
details: Consistency here means constraints, not the distributed-systems meaning of 'every replica agrees'. Those are different words that share a spelling.
examples: A transfer that cannot leave only one account changed
A commit that is still present after the database restarts

definition: An activation function is the nonlinearity applied to a layer's weighted sum. It lets the network represent relationships that are not straight lines. ReLU, which outputs zero for negative inputs and the input otherwise, is the common choice in hidden layers.
examples: ReLU in a hidden layer
A softmax that turns scores into a distribution over classes

definition: An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, the list of vertices it connects to. Space grows with the number of vertices plus edges, which suits sparse graphs. Finding whether one particular edge exists takes time proportional to that vertex's degree.

complexity.time: Listing neighbors is proportional to the degree. Checking one edge is O(degree).
complexity.space: O(V + E).

examples: A social graph with few edges per person
A road map stored for breadth-first search

definition: An adjacency matrix stores a graph as a table indexed by vertex pairs. The cell for (u, v) says whether that edge exists, or what it weighs. Checking one edge is constant time, and the table uses space proportional to the square of the vertex count, so it suits dense graphs.

complexity.time: Edge lookup is O(1). Listing all neighbors of a vertex is O(V).

examples: A small densely connected network
Floyd-Warshall, which updates a matrix of distances

definition: An agent, in this sense, is a loop in which a model chooses actions, observes their results, and continues until a goal is met or a limit is reached. Tool calling is the usual way it acts. The loop needs a budget, because nothing inside the model guarantees that it will stop.
prompt: What is an agent built on a language model?
examples: A loop that searches, reads a result, and searches again
A coding assistant that edits a file and then runs a test

definition: Aggregation is a has-a relationship in which the contained object can outlive the container. The container uses the part and does not own its lifetime. It is a weaker link than composition.
examples: A university that aggregates students who exist independently
A playlist that refers to songs stored elsewhere

definition: Ahead-of-time compilation translates the program to machine code before it runs. Startup does not include a compile step, and the compiler cannot use measurements from the current run. Traditional compiled languages work this way.
examples: A release binary produced by a C compiler
A build step that emits native code for a whole program

definition: Alerting notifies a person when a monitoring rule says something needs attention. A useful alert is actionable and rare enough to be believed. An alert that fires constantly, or that nobody can act on, trains people to ignore alerts.
examples: A page when the error budget is being burned quickly
A ticket when disk space will run out within a day

definition: An algorithm is a finite procedure that solves a class of problems. Each step is definite, and the procedure ends for the inputs it claims to handle. The same algorithm can be written in many languages; the steps, not the syntax, are the idea.
examples: A recipe for finding an item in a sorted list
A procedure for scheduling tasks onto machines

definition: The arithmetic logic unit is the part of the processor that computes: addition, subtraction, comparisons, and bitwise operations. The rest of the CPU feeds it operands from registers and writes the result back. It does not fetch instructions or talk to main memory by itself.
examples: Adding two registers
Computing a bitwise and of two values

definition: Anti-aliasing reduces the jagged edges that appear when a continuous edge is forced onto a pixel grid. It blends coverage at the boundary instead of painting each pixel fully inside or fully outside. The cost is extra samples or extra work per pixel.
examples: A diagonal line that looks smooth rather than stair-stepped
Multisample anti-aliasing on a triangle edge

definition: An API is the set of operations a piece of software offers its callers, and the rules for using them. It may be functions in a library or requests sent to a service. Callers rely on that surface staying stable when the internals change.
examples: The public functions of a library
An HTTP API for creating and listing orders

definition: API design is the practice of choosing the operations, names, errors, and compatibility rules that callers will depend on. A good API is small, consistent, and hard to misuse. Once it is published, changing it is expensive, so the design includes how it will evolve.
examples: Choosing nouns and HTTP methods for a resource
Deciding that a missing resource is a not-found error rather than an empty success

definition: An argument is the value passed to a function at a call. It is matched to a parameter by position or by name. Reassigning the parameter does not change the caller's variable, though mutating a shared object is visible to the caller.
examples: The two numbers passed to a max function
A named argument that skips an optional parameter

definition: ARP resolves an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local network. A host asks who has the IP address, and the owner answers with its MAC address. The result is cached so later frames can be addressed without asking again.
examples: Finding the MAC address of the local router
A cached mapping used for the next packet to that host

definition: An array stores elements in contiguous positions and identifies each one by an index. Reading or writing an element by index is constant time. Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts the elements that follow, so that cost grows with the length.

complexity.time: Index access is O(1). Search is O(n) unless the array is sorted. Insert or delete in the middle is O(n).
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: A list of the last 100 readings, addressed by position
The rows of a matrix stored in one contiguous block

definition: Artificial intelligence is the effort to build systems that perform tasks we associate with judgment, perception, or language. It includes both hand-written rules and systems that learn from data. In current practice, most of the progress people mean by the term comes from machine learning.
examples: A system that transcribes speech
A program that plays a game by search

definition: Assembly is a human-readable text form of machine code, with a mnemonic for each instruction. An assembler translates it to machine code almost one line per instruction. People use it to see what a compiler emitted, or to write a tiny piece of code the compiler cannot express.
examples: A mnemonic add instruction with register operands
Compiler output inspected while chasing a bug

definition: Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair. Data encrypted with the public key is decrypted with the private key, so anyone can encrypt to a recipient and only the recipient can read it. It is slower than symmetric encryption and is usually used to protect a symmetric key rather than a large payload.
examples: RSA
Elliptic-curve encryption of a session key

definition: Async/await is syntax for asynchronous code that reads as a sequence of steps. An async function can pause at await until a promise settles, then continue with the result. The pause suspends that function; it does not block the whole thread on the wait.
details: The function returns a promise of its own. A failure in an awaited promise rejects that returned promise unless it is handled.
examples: Awaiting a database query before using the rows
Awaiting two independent requests one after another

definition: The attack surface is the set of places an outsider can interact with a system: endpoints, parsers, accounts, and exposed services. A larger surface gives more places for a mistake to be reachable. Reducing it means exposing fewer entry points and fewer privileges behind each one.
examples: An administrative port reachable from the internet
A parser that accepts file uploads from anyone

definition: Attention computes, for each item in a sequence, a weighted mix of the other items. The weights say how much that item should depend on each of the others for this layer. It is the operation a transformer uses to move information between tokens.
prompt: What is attention in a neural network?
examples: A translation model focusing on the source word being translated
A token attending to an earlier token that names its subject

definition: Authentication establishes who is making a request. The usual evidence is something the party knows, has, or is, checked against a stored record. A request that has not authenticated is anonymous, whatever it claims in an unsigned field.
examples: A password checked against a stored hash
A signed token that identifies the account

definition: Authorization decides what an already identified party is allowed to do. It runs after authentication: knowing who someone is does not by itself grant access. The check is against permissions, roles, or a policy for the specific action and resource.
examples: Allowing the owner of a document to edit it
Refusing a signed-in user who is not an administrator

definition: Availability is the fraction of time a system can accept and serve work. It is often stated in nines: three nines, 99.9 percent, is a bit under nine hours of downtime a year. A system can be available and still return wrong results, which is a reliability problem rather than an availability one.
prompt: What is availability for a service?
examples: A service that answers health checks and traffic
A failover that keeps the service answering while one node is down

definition: An AVL tree is a binary search tree that rebalances after every insert and delete so the heights of a node's two subtrees differ by at most one. Rotations restore that balance. Search, insert, and delete are logarithmic in the worst case, at the cost of more rotations than a red-black tree.

complexity.time: Search, insert, and delete are O(log n) in the worst case.
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: An ordered index that must not degrade after sorted inserts

definition: The backend is the part of a web application that runs on a server and owns the rules and the data. Clients send it requests and trust its answers. It is where authorization and durable writes belong.
examples: An API that stores orders
A server that decides whether a request is allowed

definition: Backoff waits between retries, and usually waits longer after each failure. The delay gives an overloaded dependency time to recover. Adding jitter, a random spread around the delay, keeps many clients from retrying at the same moment.
examples: Waits of 100 ms, then 200 ms, then 400 ms
Jitter so a fleet of clients does not retry in lockstep

definition: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter by the chain rule, starting at the output and moving back through the layers. It is how a deep network knows which way to adjust an early weight. It is a way to compute the gradient, not a separate learning rule from gradient descent.
examples: Gradients flowing from a classification loss back to the first layer
A framework recording operations so it can differentiate them

definition: Backtracking searches by trying a choice, recursing, and undoing that choice when it cannot lead to a solution. It explores a tree of partial solutions and prunes a branch as soon as the partial solution is invalid. It is correct for many combinatorial problems and can still be exponential.
examples: Placing queens so that no two share a row, column, or diagonal
Filling a sudoku grid
Generating permutations

definition: Backward compatibility means a new version still works for callers or data written against an older version. Adding an optional field is usually compatible; removing or redefining an existing one is not. It is what lets other people upgrade without changing their code at the same moment.
examples: An API that still accepts the old request and also a new optional field
A file format a new version can still read

definition: Behavior-driven development describes expected behavior in examples phrased in the language of the problem, often given-when-then. The examples are executable specifications. The emphasis is on the behavior a stakeholder would recognize, not on the structure of the code.
examples: Given an empty cart, when an item is added, then the total is the item's price
A scenario shared by a developer and a product owner

definition: Bellman-Ford finds shortest paths from one source and allows negative edge weights. It relaxes every edge once per vertex, repeating that pass |V| - 1 times. A further pass that still improves a distance means the graph has a negative cycle reachable from the source.

complexity.time: O(V * E).
complexity.space: O(V) for the distances.

examples: A currency graph where an exchange rate can act like a negative edge
Detecting a negative cycle that would make a 'shortest' path undefined

definition: Big-O describes an upper bound on how a cost grows as the input grows. Engineers usually state the worst-case cost this way, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. It is an upper bound, so a tighter description may exist.
details: People often say O when they mean a tight bound. Big-Theta is the notation for a bound that is both upper and lower.
O(2n) and O(n) are the same class. The constant factor is dropped.
examples: Linear search is O(n)
A doubly nested loop over the same n items is O(n^2)

definition: Big-Omega describes a lower bound on how a cost grows. It says the cost is at least on the order of the stated function. A matching Big-O and Big-Omega together are a Big-Theta bound.
examples: Any comparison sort is Omega(n log n) in the worst case
Reading n inputs is Omega(n)

definition: Big-Theta describes a tight bound: the cost grows no faster and no slower than the stated function, up to a constant factor. It is both an upper bound and a lower bound. When people say an algorithm 'is' n log n, this is the claim they usually mean.
examples: Merge sort is Theta(n log n) in the worst case
A single loop from 1 to n is Theta(n)

definition: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array by repeatedly cutting the remaining range in half. Each step compares the middle element and discards the half that cannot contain the target. The input must be sorted, and index access must be constant time.
details: On duplicates, the basic form may return any match. A left-biased or right-biased version finds the first or last match.
The middle index is computed as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 so the sum cannot overflow a fixed-width integer.

complexity.time: O(log n).
complexity.space: O(1) for the iterative form. O(log n) if written as recursion.

examples: Looking up a word in a sorted dictionary
Finding the insertion point for a new key in a sorted array
sketch:
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo <= hi:
  mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
  if a[mid] == target: return mid
  if a[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
  else: hi = mid - 1
return not found

definition: A binary search tree is a binary tree kept in order: every value in a node's left subtree is less than the node, and every value in the right subtree is greater. Search, insert, and delete follow one path from the root. That path stays short only while the tree stays balanced.
details: Inserting values in sorted order can stretch the tree into a chain. Every operation is then linear.
Equal keys need a chosen rule: forbid them, keep them on one side, or store a count in the node.

complexity.time: Search, insert, and delete are O(h), where h is the height. That is O(log n) when balanced and O(n) in the worst case.
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: An ordered set of timestamps
A map from names to values kept in key order

definition: A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most two children, usually called left and right. The shape alone does not say how values are ordered. It is the shape used by search trees, heaps, and expression trees.

complexity.time: Visiting every node is O(n).
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: An expression tree for 1 + 2 * 3
A tournament bracket

definition: Bit manipulation changes a number by operating on its individual bits. And, or, and xor combine two bit patterns; shifts move bits left or right; a mask isolates the bits you care about. Programs use it for flags, sets of small integers, and arithmetic that stays inside one machine word.
details: Shifting left by k multiplies an unsigned value by 2^k. An arithmetic right shift fills with the sign bit; a logical right shift fills with zero.
Xor of a value with itself is zero, and xor with zero leaves a value unchanged.
examples: A permissions word where each bit is one permission
Testing whether the kth bit of a number is set

definition: A blue-green deployment keeps two complete environments, one serving traffic and one idle with the new version. The switch sends traffic to the new environment once it is ready. Switching back sends traffic to the old environment if the new one misbehaves.
examples: Two identical stacks, with the load balancer pointing at one
An immediate return to the previous stack

definition: A boolean is a value that is either true or false. Comparisons and logical tests produce booleans, and conditionals use them to choose a branch. They combine with and, or, and not.
examples: The result of checking whether a list is empty
A flag that records whether a user is signed in

definition: Boolean logic is the algebra of true and false. And is true only when both inputs are true, or is true when at least one input is true, and not reverses a value. Programs use it in conditions, and processors use the same operations on bits.
details: De Morgan's laws: not (A and B) is (not A) or (not B), and not (A or B) is (not A) and (not B).

definition: A branch is a named pointer to a commit, and it moves forward as new commits are added on that line of work. It is a label, not a separate copy of the files. Several branches can exist so different lines of work do not have to share a tip.
prompt: What is a Git branch?
examples: A feature branch that points at the latest commit of that feature
The main branch that releases are cut from

definition: Branch prediction guesses which way a conditional branch will go so the pipeline can keep fetching instead of waiting. A correct guess costs nothing extra. A wrong guess flushes the work that was fetched along the wrong path.
examples: Predicting that a loop branch will be taken again
A misprediction at the end of the loop

definition: Breadth-first search explores a graph in layers, visiting every neighbor of the current layer before going deeper. It uses a queue so the oldest discovered vertex is expanded next. On an unweighted graph, the first time it reaches a vertex is along a shortest path by number of edges.
details: A seen set is required, or a cycle makes the search run forever.
On a tree there is no cycle, but the seen set still avoids nothing extra if each node has one parent.

complexity.time: O(V + E) with an adjacency list.
complexity.space: O(V) for the queue and the seen set.

examples: The fewest hops between two people in a social graph
Spreading a flood fill one ring at a time

definition: Bubble sort walks the list repeatedly and swaps neighbors that are out of order. Each pass moves the next extreme element to its final end. It is easy to see and rarely used for real data, because it stays quadratic unless the input is already nearly sorted and the implementation stops early.
details: The usual implementation is stable.
A pass with no swaps means the list is sorted and later passes can be skipped.

complexity.time: O(n^2) worst and average. O(n) best case if it stops when a pass makes no swaps.
complexity.space: O(1) extra space.

examples: A classroom demonstration of swapping neighbors

definition: A buffer overflow writes past the end of a fixed block of memory and overwrites whatever follows it. The risk is corrupted data or, in an unsafe language, a change in what the program does next. The defense is bounds checking, a memory-safe language, and compiler protections that block the write.
examples: A bounds-checked copy into a fixed buffer
Code written in a language that refuses an out-of-range write

definition: A build system turns source into artifacts by running the right tools in the right order. It tracks which inputs each output depends on, so a change rebuilds only what is affected. Make, and the build tools behind compiled languages, are build systems.
examples: Recompiling only the files that changed
Producing a packaged artifact from source and assets

definition: Bytecode is an instruction set designed for a virtual machine rather than for a physical CPU. A compiler emits it, and the virtual machine executes it, often with a further just-in-time compilation to machine code. It is portable across machines that provide the same virtual machine.
examples: Java bytecode
Python bytecode executed by its virtual machine

definition: A cache stores a copy of data closer to where it is used, so a repeated access avoids a slower source. A hit is a use of that copy; a miss fetches from the slower source and usually fills the cache. Caches help only when the same data, or nearby data, is used again soon.
details: A CPU cache copies memory. A database or HTTP cache copies query results or responses. The idea is the same.
Invalidation is the hard part: a cached copy must not be served after the source has changed, or the system must accept that it might be.
examples: An L1 cache in front of main memory
A cached result of an expensive query

definition: The call stack stores one frame per active function call: a return address, saved registers, parameters, and local variables. A call pushes a frame and a return pops it, so calls finish in the reverse of the order they started. Running out of stack space is a stack overflow.
details: People say 'the stack' for this region. It is one use of the stack data structure, not the definition of that structure.
examples: Nested function calls
Local variables that disappear when the function returns

definition: A callback is a function passed into another function so it can be called later, when a result is ready or an event happens. The caller decides what to do; the callee decides when. It is the basic way to continue after asynchronous work.
examples: A function run when a timer fires
A comparison function passed to a sort

definition: A calling convention is the part of an ABI that says how a function is called: which registers hold arguments, who saves which registers, and how the stack is cleaned up. Caller and callee must agree, or the arguments are read from the wrong place. It is a binary rule, not a feature of the source language's syntax.
examples: The first few arguments passed in registers
A callee-saved register that a function must restore

definition: A canary deployment sends a small share of traffic to the new version and watches it before shifting the rest. A problem affects only that share. The rollout grows if the signals stay healthy, and stops if they do not.
examples: Five percent of requests routed to a new version
A rollout halted because the error rate rose

definition: The CAP theorem says a distributed store cannot guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance all at once. During a network partition it must choose between answering every request and making every answer reflect the latest write. Real networks partition, so the practical question is how the system behaves while a partition lasts.
details: Consistency in CAP means every read sees the latest write. That is not the C in ACID, which means database constraints.
examples: A system that rejects writes during a partition so replicas do not diverge
A system that keeps accepting writes and reconciles them later

definition: A CDN stores copies of content at many locations and serves a user from a nearby one. The origin is contacted when the nearby copy misses or expires. It cuts latency for static content and absorbs load that would otherwise hit the origin.
examples: An image served from a location near the user
A cached copy of a script that many pages share

definition: A certificate binds a name to a public key and is signed by an issuer. A verifier who trusts the issuer can trust that binding. On the web, a server's certificate says which name its key belongs to, and the client checks that the name matches the site it asked for.
examples: A certificate for a website's name
A signature from a certificate authority on that certificate

definition: Cherry-pick copies one commit's change onto the current branch as a new commit. The new commit has a different hash and the current branch as its parent. It is how a single fix moves to a release branch without merging everything else.
prompt: What does git cherry-pick do?
examples: Copying one bug fix onto a release branch
Replaying a commit that landed on the wrong branch

definition: The CIA triad names three security goals: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Confidentiality means the wrong party cannot read the data. Integrity means it cannot be changed without detection. Availability means the legitimate party can get to it when needed.
examples: Encryption supporting confidentiality
A signature supporting integrity
Redundancy supporting availability

definition: CIDR is the notation for an IP prefix: an address followed by the number of leading bits that identify the network. 10.0.0.0/8 means the first 8 bits are the network. Routing tables and firewall rules are written in that form.
examples: A firewall rule that allows one prefix

definition: A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is failing, for a period, instead of waiting on every request. While it is open, callers fail fast or take a fallback. After a pause it allows a trial request, and it closes again if that request succeeds.
examples: Skipping a down recommendation service and showing a default list
A client that fails fast instead of piling up timeouts

definition: A class is a definition of a kind of object: the data it holds and the methods that operate on that data. It is the template. Creating an object from the class produces an instance with its own data.
prompt: What is a class in object-oriented programming?
examples: A User class with a name and a method that changes the password
A Shape class that declares an area method

definition: A client is the program that initiates a request. It asks for work or data and consumes the response. A browser is a client of a web server, and a web server can itself be a client of a database.
examples: A browser
A mobile app calling an API
A service calling another service

definition: Client-server is an arrangement where clients request work and a server performs it and responds. The server holds the shared resource or the authority. Many clients share one server, or a tier of servers.
examples: Browsers requesting pages from a web server
Applications querying a database server

definition: A closure is a function together with the bindings from the scope where it was created. When the function runs later, it can still read those captured variables, even after the outer call has returned. That is how a callback remembers the context it was built in.
details: If the captured variable is mutable, every closure that captured it sees later assignments, not a private copy from creation time. Languages differ on whether the loop variable in a closure is shared.
examples: A function that returns another function which still sees a local counter
An event handler that remembers the button that created it

definition: Code coverage measures which parts of the code ran during tests: lines, branches, or paths. A high number means the tests executed that code, not that they checked the right things. A low number on a critical branch is a prompt to add a test.
examples: Line coverage of a module
Branch coverage showing an error path never ran

definition: A code review is another person reading a change before it is merged, looking for defects, unclear design, and missing tests. The author keeps responsibility for the change. The review spreads knowledge of the code beyond the person who wrote it.
examples: Comments on a pull request before it is merged
A checklist that asks whether error paths were considered

definition: A code smell is a surface sign that the design may be weak, not a defect by itself. A very long method, or a type that is modified for many unrelated reasons, is a smell. It is a prompt to look, not a proof that the code is wrong.
examples: A function with dozens of parameters
Duplicated logic that has already started to drift apart

definition: Cohesion is how closely the responsibilities inside a module belong together. High cohesion means the module is about one thing. Low cohesion means unrelated jobs were placed together and will change for unrelated reasons.
examples: A date module that only deals with dates
A utilities module that mixes string, file, and network helpers

definition: A column is one attribute of a table, with a name and a type, present on every row. A row stores one value for that column, which may be null if the schema allows it. Queries project the columns they want and filter on column values.
prompt: What is a column in a relational database?
examples: An email column of text
A created-at column of timestamps

definition: Command injection happens when untrusted text is placed into a shell command and the shell interprets it as syntax. The risk is the program running commands its author did not write. The defense is to avoid a shell and to pass the program and its arguments as separate values.
examples: Starting a process with an argument array rather than a shell string
Refusing to pass user input through a command interpreter

definition: A commit is one recorded snapshot in the history, with a message, an author, a timestamp, and pointers to its parent commits. Changing a commit does not edit it in place; it creates a new commit with a new identity. The identity is a hash of the contents, so two clones agree on what that commit is.
prompt: What is a Git commit?
examples: A snapshot with the message 'Fix the empty-cart total'
A merge commit with two parents

definition: A compiler translates a program from a source language into a lower-level form, usually machine code or bytecode. It checks the program and then generates the output a machine or a virtual machine can run. Once compiled, the program can run without the compiler.
examples: A C compiler emitting machine code
A compiler emitting bytecode for a virtual machine

definition: A composite index is an index on several columns in a stated order. A query can use it for a prefix of that order: the leading column, or the leading columns together. A filter on a later column alone does not get the index's full benefit.
details: An index on (last_name, first_name) serves a search by last name, and a search by both. It does not efficiently serve a search by first name alone.
examples: An index on (customer_id, created_at) for one customer's recent orders

definition: Composition builds an object by giving it other objects as parts, and the whole owns those parts. When the whole goes away, the parts go with it. Behavior is reused by containing a collaborator instead of inheriting from it.
examples: A car that contains an engine it owns
A service object that contains the repository it uses

definition: Concurrency is dealing with several tasks whose execution overlaps in time. They may take turns on one processor, or they may run truly in parallel. The hard part is shared state and the ordering of their steps, not the number of processors.
examples: A server with many requests in flight on one machine
An application that downloads data while the user keeps typing

definition: A connection pool keeps a set of open database connections and lends them to requests. Opening a connection is expensive, so reusing one avoids that cost on every query. The pool's size limits how many queries run at once, and a request must return its connection when it finishes.
examples: A web server lending a connection per request
A pool that waits when every connection is already checked out

definition: Consensus is getting a set of nodes to agree on a single value, or on a sequence of values, even when some nodes fail. It is how a cluster agrees on a log of operations. Paxos and Raft are standard algorithms, and they cannot make progress if too many nodes are unavailable.
examples: A cluster agreeing on the next entry in a replicated log
Electing which node may commit writes

definition: A constant is a named binding the program does not reassign. It gives one stable name to a value so the rest of the code does not repeat it or change it by accident. In some languages the binding is fixed, but the object it points at can still be modified.
details: A constant binding and an immutable value are different promises. The first forbids reassignment; the second forbids changing the value itself.
examples: A maximum retry count
The number of bytes in a kilobyte the program uses

definition: A constructor is the procedure that runs when a new instance is created. It sets the instance's starting fields and can reject input that would make an invalid object. After it returns, the caller holds a usable instance.
examples: A User constructor that requires a non-empty email
A connection constructor that opens the underlying socket

definition: A container is a process, or a small group of processes, isolated with operating-system features such as namespaces and resource limits. It shares the host kernel and does not boot its own. An image supplies the filesystem and the starting command.
examples: An application process with its own filesystem view
Several containers on one machine, each with a limited CPU share

definition: A container image is a filesystem snapshot plus metadata, including the command to run, used to start a container. Images are built in layers and identified by a digest of their contents. A running container adds a writable layer on top; the image itself stays unchanged.
prompt: What is a container image?
examples: An image tagged as a particular release
A digest that identifies the exact bytes that were deployed

definition: A container registry stores images and serves them to the machines that run containers. A deploy pulls an image by name and tag, or by digest. The registry is the distribution point, not the place the container runs.
examples: A CI job pushing an image after a successful build
A cluster pulling that image onto a node

definition: A context switch saves the processor state of the running thread and restores the state of another, so the processor can run that other thread. The saved state includes registers and the instruction pointer. Switches are necessary for sharing a processor, and they cost time that does no application work.
examples: The scheduler pausing one process to run another
Switching from a user thread into the kernel on a system call

definition: The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can take into account at once, including the prompt and the generated output. Text beyond that window is not visible to the model unless something else brings it back in. Longer windows cost more compute and memory.
examples: A model that can see 8,000 tokens of conversation
A document truncated because it does not fit

definition: Continuous delivery keeps the main branch in a state that can be released at any time. An automated pipeline produces a releasable artifact after the tests pass. Releasing that artifact can still be a human decision.
examples: A build that produces a versioned artifact ready for production
A release that is a button press rather than a fresh build

definition: Continuous deployment goes one step past continuous delivery: every change that passes the pipeline is deployed to production automatically. There is no separate human release step. It requires a pipeline trustworthy enough that a passing build is safe to ship.
examples: A merge to main that reaches production without a release meeting
An automatic rollback when health checks fail after a deploy

definition: Continuous integration is the practice of merging work into a shared branch often, and automatically building and testing each change. Failures show up against a small change instead of against a long-lived branch. The shared branch is expected to stay in a working state.
examples: A pipeline that runs tests on every pull request
A broken build that blocks the merge

definition: A cookie is a small value a server asks a browser to store and to send back on later requests to that site. It is the usual place a session identifier lives. Flags limit it: Secure sends it only over HTTPS, HttpOnly keeps script from reading it, and SameSite limits when it is sent on a request that came from another site.
examples: A session id cookie
A preference cookie that is not an authentication secret

definition: CORS is the browser rule for when a page from one origin may read a response from another origin. The browser asks, through headers, and the server answers whether that origin is allowed. It is a browser protection, not a boundary the server can rely on, because a non-browser client ignores it.
examples: A page on one site reading an API on another
A response header that names the allowed origin

definition: Counting sort orders integers that fall in a limited range by counting how many times each value appears, then writing them back out from those counts. It is not a comparison sort, so it can beat the n log n comparison lower bound. The range has to be modest, because the count array is as large as the range.
details: Implemented by placing values according to prefix sums of the counts, it is stable.

complexity.time: O(n + k), where k is the size of the value range.
complexity.space: O(k) for the counts, plus O(n) if the output is a separate array.

examples: Sorting exam scores that only range from 0 to 100
Sorting small integers as one pass of radix sort

definition: Coupling is the degree to which one module depends on the internals of another. Tight coupling means a change in one forces changes in the other. Loose coupling, usually through a small interface, lets each side change on its own.
examples: A caller that constructs a concrete database class, coupled to that class
A caller that depends only on an interface, coupled to the contract

definition: A CPU is the processor that fetches, decodes, and executes instructions. It performs arithmetic, makes branches, and moves data between registers and memory. A modern chip contains several cores, each able to run its own instruction stream.
examples: A core executing a thread's instructions
A chip with several cores sharing one memory system

definition: Cross-site request forgery happens when a browser attaches a user's credentials, such as a cookie, to a request the user did not intend, initiated from another site. The risk is an action performed while the user is signed in. The defense is a secret the other site cannot read, together with SameSite cookies on the session.
examples: A state-changing request that requires a per-session token
A session cookie marked SameSite

definition: Cross-site scripting happens when a page treats untrusted text as code and the browser runs it in the user's session with that site. The risk is a script that can act as the user. The defense is to encode text for the context it is inserted into, and to rely on a framework's escaping rather than inserting raw markup.
examples: Text inserted as text, not as HTML
A framework that escapes values in a template by default

definition: A cryptographic hash maps data to a fixed-size digest so that a change in the data changes the digest, and the data cannot practically be recovered from the digest. It is used to detect tampering and to identify content. A hash built for hash tables does not make these promises and is the wrong tool here.
details: A collision is two inputs with the same digest. A cryptographic hash is designed so finding one is not feasible.
SHA-256 is a general cryptographic hash. Password storage wants a slow password hash instead.
examples: A digest used to detect that a file changed
A commit id that is a hash of the commit's contents

definition: A data type classifies values and says which operations are allowed on them. Integers, floating-point numbers, booleans, and text are common examples. The type tells the compiler or the runtime how to store a value and what it may do with it.
examples: An integer, which supports arithmetic
A string, which supports concatenation and indexing

definition: A database is an organized store of data with a way to query and update it, usually used by many programs at once. It handles durability, concurrent access, and structure so each application does not invent those itself. The database management system is the software that provides that store.
examples: A store of accounts and orders
A service that many application instances query

definition: A database lock reserves a row, a range, or a table so concurrent transactions do not make conflicting changes. A writer typically takes an exclusive lock; readers may share. Locks held in inconsistent orders are a common cause of deadlock.
prompt: What is a database lock?
examples: A row lock during an update
A lock that makes a second transaction wait

definition: A deadlock is a set of threads or transactions that are all waiting, each holding a resource another one needs, so none can proceed. It requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption of the resources, and a circular wait. Breaking any one of those conditions prevents that deadlock.
examples: Thread A holding lock 1 and waiting for lock 2, while thread B does the opposite
Two database transactions locking rows in opposite orders

definition: Defense in depth uses more than one independent control so a single failure does not fully expose the system. A check at the edge and a check at the data store are two layers. The layers have to be able to fail separately; two copies of the same check are not two layers.
examples: A network rule plus an authorization check in the application
Encryption plus access control

definition: Denormalization stores a fact in more than one place on purpose, usually so a read can avoid a join or a second lookup. Writes become harder, because every copy must be updated. It is a performance trade against a normalized design, not the default starting point.
examples: A copy of the author's name stored on each post
A counter maintained on a parent row instead of counted from children

definition: Dependency injection means a unit receives the collaborators it needs instead of constructing them itself. The caller, or a container, passes them in through a constructor or a parameter. The unit stays focused on its job, and a test can pass a substitute.
examples: A service constructed with a repository argument
A test that passes a fake clock instead of the system clock

definition: The dependency inversion principle says high-level code should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level classes. The concrete class depends on that abstraction as well and is supplied from outside. Dependency injection is a common way to wire the concrete class in.
examples: Business logic that calls a Repository interface, with a database class implementing it
A notifier interface, with email and SMS as interchangeable implementations

definition: Dependency management is declaring, resolving, and updating the libraries a project uses. A manifest names the dependencies, and a lockfile records the exact versions that were resolved. Updating is a deliberate change, because a new version can change behavior.
examples: A manifest that requires a logging library and a lockfile that pins its version
A tool that reports a known-bad version of a dependency

definition: A deployment is the act of putting a built version of software into an environment where it runs. It is distinct from the build that produced the artifact. A successful deployment leaves the new version serving traffic, or leaves the previous version in place if it aborts.
examples: Releasing a new image to production
Shipping a build to a staging environment first

definition: Depth-first search follows one path as far as it can, then backtracks and tries the next unused edge. It uses a stack, either an explicit one or the call stack of recursion. It classifies edges and finds structure such as finish times, which topological sort and cycle detection use.
details: A seen set, or a color for visiting versus finished, is required on graphs that may contain cycles.
The order of neighbors changes which path is followed first. It does not change the O(V + E) cost.

complexity.time: O(V + E) with an adjacency list.
complexity.space: O(V) for the stack and the seen set.

examples: Detecting a cycle in a directed graph
Solving a maze by following one corridor until it ends

definition: A deque is a double-ended queue: elements can be added or removed at either end in constant time. It can act as a stack, a queue, or a window that slides from both sides. A circular buffer or a doubly linked list is the usual backing store.

complexity.time: Add and remove at either end are O(1).
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: A sliding window that drops items from the front and adds at the back
An undo stack that can also peek at the oldest item

definition: DHCP assigns a host its IP configuration when it joins a network: an address, a subnet mask, a gateway, and usually DNS servers. The assignment is a lease that expires and can be renewed. It saves every machine from being configured by hand.
examples: A laptop receiving an address when it joins a network
A lease that is renewed before it expires

definition: A digital signature is produced with a private key so that anyone with the matching public key can check it. A valid signature means the data has not been altered and was signed by the holder of that private key. It provides integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality.
examples: A signed software release
A signature on a token that a server verifies

definition: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from one source in a graph with non-negative edge weights. It grows a set of settled vertices, always settling next the unsettled vertex with the smallest known distance, which a priority queue can supply. A negative edge can make a settled distance wrong, so the algorithm does not allow them.

complexity.time: O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.
complexity.space: O(V) for distances and the queue.

examples: Driving directions on roads with non-negative lengths
Least-cost routing when no link has a negative cost

definition: A directed graph gives each edge a direction, from one vertex to another. A path has to follow that direction. The reverse of an edge is a different edge, and it may not exist.
examples: Web pages and the links from one page to another
Course prerequisites that point from a later course to an earlier one

definition: A distributed system is a system whose parts run on multiple computers and cooperate by sending messages. The parts fail independently, and the network between them is slow and sometimes broken. Those two facts are what make it different from one program on one machine.
examples: A web tier plus a separate database
A storage system spread across a cluster

definition: A distributed transaction is a transaction whose writes span more than one service or database. Two-phase commit coordinates them: every participant prepares, then all commit, or all abort. It is often avoided, because a slow or failed participant blocks the others, in favor of smaller local transactions plus compensation.
examples: Two databases committing one logical update together
A saga that undoes an earlier step when a later step fails

definition: Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller independent subproblems, solves those, and combines the results. The subproblems are usually the same problem on a smaller input. Merge sort, quick sort, and binary search are standard examples.
examples: Sorting by sorting two halves and merging them
Finding a key by discarding half of a sorted array

definition: DNS translates human-readable names into the addresses and other records programs actually connect to. Resolution walks a hierarchy of servers, from the root toward the server responsible for that name. A record has a time to live, after which the answer is looked up again.
details: An A record holds an IPv4 address and an AAAA record an IPv6 address. A CNAME is an alias to another name.
examples: Turning a site name into an IP address
A mail exchanger record for a domain

definition: Documentation is writing that explains a system to a reader who is not currently inside the code. Reference documentation says what each part does; a guide says how to accomplish a task. It stays useful only when it is updated with the behavior it describes.
examples: A reference page for each public function
A guide that walks through the first successful call to an API

definition: A doubly linked list gives each node a pointer to the next node and a pointer to the previous one. The list can be walked in either direction, and a known node can be removed without first searching for its predecessor. The extra pointer costs memory on every node.

complexity.time: Access by position is O(n). Insert or delete at a known node is O(1).
complexity.space: O(n), with two pointers per node.

examples: A browser history that moves backward and forward
An ordered queue of tasks where any known task can be removed

definition: DRY, don't repeat yourself, says a single fact or rule should have one representation in the system. A change to that fact then happens in one place. Applying it to code that merely looks similar, but changes for different reasons, creates coupling rather than removing duplication.
examples: One function for a tax rule used by every caller
A shared constant for a limit that several modules enforce

definition: A dynamic array is an array that grows when it fills up. The implementation allocates a larger block, copies the old elements across, and then continues. Appending is constant time on average because resizing happens rarely and doubles the capacity.
details: A single append that triggers a resize copies every element, so that one call is linear. Averaged over a long series of appends, each append is constant time.
Some languages call this a vector or a list. Those names also mean other things.

complexity.time: Index access is O(1). Append is amortized O(1). Insert in the middle is O(n).
complexity.space: O(n), plus unused capacity in the allocated block.

examples: A list of search results that grows as matches are found
The backing store of a resizable buffer

definition: Dynamic programming solves a problem by solving overlapping subproblems and reusing those answers, relying on optimal substructure. Top-down, the program recurses and caches. Bottom-up, it fills a table from smaller subproblems to larger ones. Without overlapping subproblems, the cache does not pay for itself.
details: Optimal substructure means a best solution contains best solutions of its subproblems.
The table's dimensions follow the parameters that identify a subproblem.
examples: Edit distance between two strings
The 0-1 knapsack problem

definition: Dynamic typing checks types when the code runs. A variable can hold values of different types at different times, and a mismatch becomes an error at the bad operation. The source usually does not declare types.
examples: A variable that first holds a number and later a string
A missing method that fails only when that line runs

definition: An embedding is a vector that represents an item so that similar items land near each other. The coordinates are learned or computed; they are not a hand-labeled feature list. Search and recommendation use the distance between embeddings as a stand-in for similarity.
examples: Word vectors in which related words are nearby
An image mapped to a vector for similarity search

definition: Encapsulation hides an object's internal data behind a small set of methods. Callers use those methods and do not depend on how the data is stored. The object can change its representation later without forcing every caller to change.
examples: A balance updated only through deposit and withdraw
A collection that never exposes the array it uses internally

definition: Encryption transforms data so that only a party with the right key can read it. The unread form is ciphertext; the original is plaintext. It provides confidentiality, and by itself it does not prove who created the message.
examples: A disk that is unreadable without its key
A connection whose payload is ciphertext on the wire

definition: An end-to-end test drives the system the way a user or a client would, through its outer interface. It checks a whole path, including the pieces in between. It is the slowest and the most brittle of the common test layers, and it covers the most ground per test.
examples: A browser test that signs in and places an order
A test that sends an HTTP request and checks the stored result

definition: Endianness is the order of the bytes that make up a multi-byte number. Big-endian stores the most significant byte first. Little-endian stores the least significant byte first. Two systems must agree on the order when they exchange raw binary numbers.
examples: A 32-bit integer written to a file
A network protocol that specifies network byte order

definition: An environment variable is a named string in a process's environment, inherited by the processes it starts. Programs read configuration such as paths and modes from it. Secrets are sometimes passed this way, and then they are visible to anything that can inspect the process.
examples: A variable naming the port a server should listen on
A path list the shell searches for programs

definition: Error handling is how a program notices a failure and chooses what happens next. Common forms are exceptions, returned error values, and types that contain either a result or an error. The point is to fail in a defined way instead of continuing with a bad value.
details: Ignoring an error and hoping for a usable value tends to move the failure somewhere harder to diagnose.
examples: A function that returns an error when input is out of range
A handler that retries a timed-out request

definition: Ethernet is the common family of link-layer technologies for local networks. It sends frames addressed by MAC address over a shared medium or a switched fabric. IP packets are carried inside those frames for one hop.
examples: A wired local network
A frame switched between two machines on the same LAN

definition: An event-driven architecture has components react to events instead of calling each other for every step. A producer records that something happened, and consumers respond. The producer does not need to know who consumes the event, and a failed consumer can catch up from the log.
examples: A payment service reacting to an order-placed event
A projection that updates a read model from a stream of events

definition: Eventual consistency means replicas may disagree for a while, and they converge once updates stop arriving. A read can return a stale value during that window. It is chosen when availability during a partition matters more than every read seeing the latest write.
examples: A profile update that appears on another region a moment later
A counter that briefly differs between replicas

definition: An exception is a signal that an operation failed and cannot finish normally. Raising it jumps to the nearest handler for that failure and unwinds the calls in between. The failure path stays separate from the path where the operation succeeds.
details: An unhandled exception stops the current unit of work. A handler can recover, record the failure, or raise a different exception.
examples: Opening a file that is not there
Dividing by zero in a language that reports it this way

definition: The expected value of a random quantity is the average it would approach over many trials, weighted by probability. It is the sum of each outcome times the probability of that outcome. Average-case cost of an algorithm is an expected value over its inputs or its random choices.
examples: The average number of comparisons in a randomized quicksort
The long-run average payout of a die roll

definition: An expression is a piece of code that produces a value, such as arithmetic, a comparison, or a function call. Expressions nest inside larger expressions. By itself, an expression does not describe a sequence of actions.
examples: A call whose result is passed into another call

definition: Fault tolerance is continuing to provide the service when parts fail. It requires redundancy: another copy, or another instance, that can take the work. The system has to detect the failure and stop using the failed part.
examples: A replica promoted when the primary stops responding
A request retried on a different instance

definition: A feature is one input variable the model sees. Choosing and transforming features decides which patterns the model is able to use. A feature that leaks the answer, or that will not be available at prediction time, produces a model that looks better than it is.
prompt: What is a feature in machine learning?
examples: The number of words in an email
The age and income columns of a table

definition: A file descriptor is a small integer a process uses to refer to an open file, socket, or pipe. The kernel keeps the real open-file state in its own table, and the integer is an index into the process's table of handles. Reads and writes name the descriptor rather than the path.
examples: Standard input, output, and error as descriptors 0, 1, and 2
A socket referred to by a number after it is opened

definition: A file system organizes data on storage as files and directories and records where each file's bytes live. It handles names, permissions, and allocation of blocks. Different file systems make different tradeoffs about crash recovery, large files, and metadata.
examples: A directory tree of source files
A journal that limits damage after a crash

definition: Fine-tuning continues training a model on a narrower dataset so it performs better at a particular task or style. The starting parameters come from the earlier, broader training. It can specialize the model and can also make it worse at tasks outside the new data.
examples: Continuing training on a company's support transcripts
Adapting a general model to a classification task

definition: A firewall filters traffic according to rules, dropping or allowing packets or connections based on attributes such as address, port, and direction. It reduces the set of ways an outsider can reach a service. A rule that allows more than the service needs widens that set again.
examples: Allowing only port 443 from the internet
Blocking outbound traffic except to known destinations

definition: A fixture is the known starting state a test relies on: data, files, or objects prepared before the assertion. Each test should be able to build the fixture it needs, or share one that no test mutates unexpectedly. A test that depends on leftover state from another test is not using a fixture; it is depending on order.
examples: A user row inserted before the test runs
A temporary directory with a known file

definition: A floating-point number approximates a real number with a sign, a significand, and an exponent. It covers a huge range of magnitudes, but many decimal fractions, including 0.1, are not exact. Equality tests and sums of money need care because of that rounding.
details: Special values include infinity and not-a-number. Not-a-number is not equal to itself.
Integers beyond the significand's width cannot all be represented exactly.
examples: A graphics coordinate
A scientific measurement with a large exponent

definition: Floyd-Warshall finds shortest paths between every pair of vertices. It tries every vertex as a possible intermediate stop and updates a distance matrix by dynamic programming. Negative edges are allowed; a negative number on the diagonal of the result means a negative cycle.

complexity.space: O(V^2) for the distance matrix.

examples: All-pairs distances in a small network
Choosing a hub that shortens travel between every pair

definition: A foreign key is a column whose values must match a key in another table, usually that table's primary key. The database rejects a value that points at a missing row, if the constraint is enforced. It is how tables state a relationship rather than only implying one.
examples: An orders.customer_id that must match a customer
A comment's post id

definition: A frame is the unit of transmission on a single link, at the layer below IP. It carries a packet across one hop and is addressed with link-layer addresses such as MAC addresses. The frame is stripped and rebuilt at each hop; the packet continues.
prompt: What is a frame in networking?
examples: An Ethernet frame on a local wire
A frame header that is discarded when the packet is routed onward

definition: A frame buffer is the memory that holds the image being drawn or the image most recently finished. Rendering writes pixels into it, and the display reads them out. A double buffer draws into one buffer while the screen shows the other, then swaps.
examples: The color buffer a frame is drawn into
A depth buffer storing how far each pixel's surface is

definition: The frontend is the part of a web application that runs on the user's side and presents the interface. It talks to the backend over HTTP or a similar protocol. It is responsible for the interaction, not for being the authority on the data.
examples: A page rendered in a browser
A client that calls an API and draws the result

definition: A function is a named block of code with inputs, a body, and usually a result. Calling it runs that body with the arguments from the call. One definition can be reused instead of copying the steps.
examples: A function that returns the larger of two numbers
A function that formats a date

definition: Fuzz testing feeds a program unexpected or mutated inputs and watches for crashes, hangs, or assertion failures. The inputs are generated or altered automatically, not written as examples. It is aimed at finding inputs the author did not think of, especially in parsers.
examples: Mutated files fed to a parser
Random bytes sent to a decoder

definition: Garbage collection automatically reclaims memory that the program can no longer reach. A tracing collector finds objects reachable from roots and frees the rest. The alternative is explicit freeing, which can free too early or not at all.
details: Reference counting frees an object when its last reference drops, and it needs a separate treatment of cycles. A tracing collector finds cycles and usually pauses the program briefly.
examples: Objects freed after the last variable referring to them goes away
A generational collector that scans new objects more often

definition: A generic is a type or function parameterized by another type. One definition works for many element types, and each use is still checked for consistency. A list of integers and a list of strings can share a single list implementation.
prompt: What is a generic type?
examples: A list that can hold any one element type
A function that returns the first item of any list

definition: Git is a distributed version-control system. Every clone holds the project's history, not only the latest files. A commit records a snapshot of the tree, and later commits point at their parent commits, forming a graph.
details: The conceptual model is a snapshot plus metadata, not a list of line edits. Storage may compress that snapshot as a delta.
examples: A local clone with the full history of a repository
A commit that points at its parent and at a tree of files

definition: Git fetch downloads commits, branches, and tags from a remote that the local repository does not have yet. It updates remote-tracking references and does not change the branch you have checked out. Integrating those commits is a separate step.
prompt: What does git fetch do?
examples: Updating origin/main without touching the local main branch
Downloading a teammate's new branch

definition: Git LFS stores large files as small pointer files inside the repository and keeps the file bytes in a separate store. Clones download the bytes for the versions they check out instead of every historical copy inside Git's object database. It is for assets that do not diff or merge as text.
examples: Video or dataset files versioned alongside the code
A pointer file in the repository and the bytes on an LFS server

definition: A merge joins two lines of history. Git finds a common ancestor and combines the changes since then, creating a merge commit when both sides have moved. When both sides changed the same region, the merge stops for a person to resolve the conflict.
prompt: What is a merge in Git?
examples: Merging a feature branch into main
A merge commit with two parents

definition: Git pull downloads new commits from a remote and integrates them into the current branch. It is a fetch followed by a merge, or by a rebase when configured that way. Unlike fetch alone, it changes the branch you are on.
prompt: What does git pull do?
examples: Updating a local main branch with commits from origin
Pulling with rebase so the local commits are replayed on top

definition: Git push uploads local commits to a remote and moves the remote branch to include them. The remote rejects the push when the remote branch contains commits the local branch does not have, and a pull is needed first. A force push overwrites that check and can discard other people's commits.
prompt: What does git push do?
examples: Publishing a feature branch to origin
Updating origin/main after a local merge

definition: A remote is a named pointer to another copy of the repository, usually on a server. Fetch, pull, and push name that copy with the remote's name. Origin is the conventional name of the remote a clone was taken from.
prompt: What is a Git remote?
examples: origin, pointing at the repository the project was cloned from
A second remote pointing at a fork

definition: Git stash sets aside uncommitted changes and restores a clean working tree. The saved changes can be reapplied later. It is a shelf for work in progress, not a commit on a branch.
prompt: What does git stash do?
examples: Shelving a half-finished edit to check out another branch
Reapplying that edit when you return

definition: A tag is a name attached to a particular commit, used to mark a point such as a release. Unlike a branch, a tag is not meant to move as new commits are added. An annotated tag also stores a message and a tagger.
prompt: What is a Git tag?
examples: The tag v1.2.0 on the commit that was released
A lightweight tag marking a known-good build

definition: A .gitignore file lists patterns of files that Git should not report as untracked. It does not remove a file that is already tracked; the file has to be untracked first. Typical entries are build output, dependencies, and local secrets.
examples: Ignoring a build directory
Ignoring local environment files that contain secrets

definition: A GPU is a processor built to run a huge number of similar operations at once. It was designed for graphics and is also used for other data-parallel work, including training neural networks. It is fast at that parallel work and poor at long chains of unpredictable branches.
examples: Shading every pixel of a frame
Multiplying large matrices

definition: Gradient descent updates parameters by stepping them in the direction that reduces the loss. The gradient says which way is up; the step goes the opposite way, scaled by the learning rate. Stochastic gradient descent estimates that gradient from a small batch of examples rather than the whole dataset.
details: A learning rate that is too large diverges. One that is too small makes training very slow.
examples: A weight updated by a small step against its gradient
A mini-batch standing in for the full dataset

definition: A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges. An edge says that two vertices are related. Graphs model networks, dependencies, and any problem whose structure is connections rather than a hierarchy.
prompt: What is a graph as a data structure?
details: A tree is a graph with no cycles and exactly one path between any two vertices, once a root is chosen.
A graph may be directed, undirected, weighted, or any mix of those.

complexity.space: O(V + E) in an adjacency list, or O(V^2) in a matrix. V is vertices and E is edges.

examples: Cities connected by roads
Tasks connected by 'must happen before' links

definition: GraphQL is a query language for APIs in which the client asks for a specific shape of data from a schema. One request can name the fields and the related objects it wants. The server resolves that selection, so clients avoid both a fixed payload and a separate endpoint for every shape.
examples: A query that asks for a user's name and the titles of their orders
A schema that defines the types a client may request

definition: A greedy algorithm builds a solution by making the locally best choice at each step and never taking it back. That produces a best overall solution only when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. When those hold, the algorithm is simple; when they do not, the locally best step can ruin the global result.
examples: Interval scheduling by always taking the job that ends soonest
Kruskal's algorithm adding the lightest safe edge

definition: Hardware multithreading lets one core keep more than one thread's state and switch between them, often to hide a stall such as a cache miss. The threads share the core's execution units. It is a hardware technique, separate from the operating system scheduling many threads onto many cores.
details: Simultaneous multithreading is the common form, where the threads share a core's execution units in the same cycle.
examples: A core running two hardware threads so one can proceed while the other waits on memory

definition: A hash table stores values under keys and finds a key by hashing it to a slot. With a good hash and a moderate load, lookup, insert, and delete average constant time. A run of collisions in one slot degrades that slot toward a linear scan.
details: The load factor is the number of keys divided by the number of slots. Growing the table and rehashing keeps the load factor down.
Keys need a stable hash and an equality test. Mutable keys that change hash after insertion are lost.

complexity.time: Average lookup, insert, and delete are O(1). Worst case is O(n) when many keys land in one slot.
complexity.space: O(n) for the entries, plus the slot array.

examples: A dictionary from user id to account
Counting how many times each word appears

definition: Hashing maps a key to a fixed-size value, called a hash, so the key can be placed or found without scanning a whole collection. A good hash for a hash table spreads keys evenly across slots. This is a different requirement from a cryptographic hash, which must also be hard to reverse and hard to collide on purpose.
prompt: What is hashing in data structures?
details: Equal keys must hash to the same slot, and the equality test still has to confirm a match.
A hash that depends on a memory address changes between runs and cannot be stored as a durable key.
examples: Choosing the slot for a key in a hash table
A checksum that detects accidental corruption of a file

definition: A health check is a probe that reports whether an instance should receive traffic. A load balancer or scheduler uses the answer to add or remove the instance. A check that only tests that the process is running can say yes while the instance cannot actually serve.
examples: An HTTP endpoint that checks the database connection
A readiness check that stays negative until startup finishes

definition: A heap is a complete binary tree that keeps its smallest element, or its largest, at the root. Every parent is ordered against its children, but siblings are not ordered against each other. The shape supports finding the extreme element immediately and inserting in logarithmic time.
prompt: What is a heap as a data structure?
details: This is not the memory heap, which is the region used for dynamic allocation. The two ideas only share a name.
In an array, the children of index i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2 when the root is at index 0.

complexity.time: Find-min is O(1). Insert and remove-min are O(log n). Building a heap from n items is O(n).
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: The pending event with the soonest time
Selecting the k smallest items without fully sorting

definition: Heap sort builds a heap from the input and then repeatedly removes the root, which is the next extreme element, into the output order. Building the heap is linear and each removal is logarithmic, so the worst case is n log n. The usual in-place version is not stable.

complexity.time: O(n log n) in the best, average, and worst cases.
complexity.space: O(1) extra space for the in-place version.

examples: A worst-case n log n sort that does not need a second array

definition: HTTP is a request-response protocol for transferring resources, used by browsers and by APIs. A request names a method and a target; a response carries a status code and a body. The protocol itself does not remember the client between requests; any session state is added by the application.
details: GET is for reading and is meant to be safe. PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent. POST is the method for actions that are not necessarily either.
Status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
examples: A browser fetching a page
A client posting JSON to an API

definition: HTTPS is HTTP sent over TLS, so the bytes of the connection are encrypted and the server is authenticated. A network observer can see that a connection exists and roughly how much data moves, not the contents or the URL path. The usual port is 443.
examples: A browser loading a site with a locked padlock
An API call whose body cannot be read on the network

definition: A hyperparameter is a choice made before training, not a value the training loop learns. Learning rate, tree depth, and the width of a layer are hyperparameters. They are chosen with validation data, not by fitting them on the training set alone.
examples: A learning rate
The number of layers in a network
A regularization strength

definition: An operation is idempotent when doing it several times has the same effect as doing it once. Retries are then safe: a lost response does not become a double charge or a double insert. The operation has to be designed that way; repeating an ordinary insert is not idempotent.
examples: Setting a record to a value, which can be repeated
A payment request carrying an idempotency key so a retry does not charge twice

definition: An immutable value cannot be changed after it is created. An update produces a new value and leaves the old one alone. Other holders of the original cannot observe a surprise change, which makes sharing safer.
details: A language can freeze a binding, freeze an object, or both. Those are different guarantees.
examples: A string that concatenation does not alter
A date value whose fields cannot be reassigned
