definition: An index is a side structure that lets the database find rows by a key without scanning the whole table. It speeds reads that match the key and slows writes, which must update the index too. An index on the wrong columns, or one that the query cannot use, only adds cost.
prompt: What is a database index?
examples: An index on users.email for login lookups
A primary-key index the engine maintains automatically

definition: Inference uses a trained model to make a prediction on an input, without updating the model's parameters. It is the model's ordinary use after training. Its cost and latency are properties of the model and the hardware, separate from how long training took.
prompt: What is inference in machine learning?
examples: Classifying one uploaded image
Generating the next tokens of a reply

definition: Infrastructure as code describes servers, networks, and policies in files that a tool applies, instead of changing them by hand. The files are reviewed and versioned like application code. Applying the same files again converges the real infrastructure toward that description.
examples: A file that declares a database and its network rules
A review of an infrastructure change before it is applied

definition: Inheritance lets a class take the fields and methods of a parent class and add or replace behavior. A subclass is meant to be usable where the parent is expected. Long chains of inheritance become brittle, so reuse is often better done by composition.
examples: A SavingsAccount class that extends Account
A specialized exception type that extends a base exception

definition: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by taking the next element and inserting it into the position where it belongs. Nearly sorted input is cheap, because each element only moves a short distance. The worst case, reverse-sorted input, compares every pair.
details: The usual implementation is stable.
It is often used for the tiny partitions inside a faster sort.

complexity.time: O(n^2) worst and average. O(n) when the input is already sorted.
complexity.space: O(1) extra space.

examples: Sorting a hand of cards
Cleaning up a list that is already almost in order

definition: An instance is an object created from a class. The class describes the shape; the instance is one concrete object with its own field values. Two instances of the same class share the method definitions and not the field values.
prompt: What is an instance in object-oriented programming?
examples: Two Date instances that happen to name the same calendar day
A new button created from a Button class

definition: An instruction is one operation the processor knows how to perform, such as adding two registers or loading a word from memory. A program is a sequence of instructions. The instruction set defines which operations exist and how they are encoded.
examples: An add of two registers
A conditional branch
A load from a memory address

definition: An instruction pipeline overlaps the stages of execution, so one instruction can be decoded while an earlier one is still executing. A typical split is fetch, decode, execute, and write back. The overlap raises throughput, and a stall happens when a later instruction needs a result that is not ready.
examples: Several instructions in different stages during one cycle
A stall while a load from memory completes

definition: An instruction set architecture is the processor's contract with software: the instructions, registers, and execution behavior that programs may rely on. Machine code is written to an ISA, not to one particular chip's internal schedule. x86-64 and ARM are two ISAs.
examples: x86-64 machine code
ARM machine code for a phone

definition: An integration test checks that several real parts work together. It might use a database, a queue, or two modules with their real boundary. Failures are broader than a unit test, and the test is usually slower.
examples: A test that saves a row and reads it back through the repository
A test of a service calling its real database

definition: Inter-process communication is how separate processes exchange data. Common mechanisms are pipes, sockets, message queues, and shared memory. Shared memory is fast and requires synchronization; message mechanisms copy data and keep the processes isolated.
examples: A pipe between a parent process and a child
Two processes communicating over a local socket

definition: An interface is a contract that names the operations a type must provide, without including that type's data. Callers depend on the interface and work with any value that meets it. Some languages also allow a default implementation for a method on the interface.
prompt: What is an interface in programming?
examples: A readable type that only requires a read method
A comparable type that only requires an ordering method

definition: The interface segregation principle says a client should not be forced to depend on methods it does not use. Several small interfaces are preferable to one wide interface. A class can implement more than one of the small ones.
examples: Splitting a Worker interface into Separate Eater and Sleeper interfaces when not every worker does both
A read-only client that depends only on a Reader interface

definition: An intermediate representation is a form of the program between source and machine code. Compilers optimize and retarget this form so each front end and each back end do not have to know about every other. LLVM IR and compiler-specific bytecode are examples.
examples: A three-address form of a function after parsing
An IR optimized before it is lowered to machine code

definition: An interpreter runs a program by executing its source, or a close representation of it, directly. There is no separate translation step that produces a machine-code binary first. The interpreter has to be present whenever the program runs.
examples: A shell executing a command
An implementation that walks an abstract syntax tree and runs it

definition: An interrupt is a signal that makes the processor stop the current instruction stream and run a handler. Hardware interrupts come from devices, such as a disk or a timer. Software interrupts and exceptions come from the running program, including system calls and faults.
examples: A timer interrupt that lets the scheduler run
A device signaling that a transfer has finished

definition: IP is the network protocol that addresses machines and routes packets between networks. A packet carries a source and a destination IP address, and routers forward it toward the destination. IP does not guarantee delivery, order, or that the payload arrives only once.
examples: A packet routed across several networks
An address that identifies a host on the internet

definition: IPv4 is the version of IP that uses 32-bit addresses, usually written as four decimal numbers. That space holds about four billion addresses, which is why sharing techniques such as NAT became common. It is still the version many networks run.
examples: An address such as 192.0.2.10
A packet with a 32-bit destination

definition: IPv6 is the version of IP that uses 128-bit addresses, written in hexadecimal. The larger space removes the shortage that shaped IPv4 practice. A host can speak one or both versions, and they are not interchangeable on the wire.
examples: A 128-bit address written in hexadecimal groups
A network that runs IPv4 and IPv6 side by side

definition: Isolation is the degree to which concurrent transactions are prevented from seeing each other's intermediate state. Stronger isolation avoids more anomalies and allows less concurrency. From weaker to stronger, the standard levels are read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, and serializable.
prompt: What is isolation in a database transaction?
details: Read uncommitted can see another transaction's uncommitted writes. Serializable behaves as if transactions ran one at a time.
examples: Read committed, which hides uncommitted work
Serializable, which prevents phantoms and other interleaving anomalies

definition: Iteration repeats a step by looping until a condition fails. The loop keeps its position and other state in variables and returns to the top, instead of calling the function again. It is the usual alternative to recursion for walking a sequence.
examples: A for loop over the indexes of an array
A while loop that reads lines until the input ends

definition: A join combines rows from two tables by a related value, usually a foreign key matching a primary key. An inner join keeps only pairs that match. A left join keeps every row of the left table and fills nulls when the right side has no match.
prompt: What is a join in SQL?
details: A right join keeps every row of the right table. A full join keeps rows from both sides. A cross join pairs every row of one table with every row of the other.
examples: Orders joined to customers on customer id
Users left-joined to profiles so users without a profile still appear

definition: JSON is a text format for structured data: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. It is the usual body of an HTTP API. It has no dates, no comments, and no distinction between integers and other numbers; those are conventions layered on top.
examples: An object of fields sent as a request body
An array of records in a response

definition: Just-in-time compilation translates code to machine code while the program is running, often after observing which parts are hot. It can optimize using information a static compiler does not have. The cost is compilation time paid during execution.
examples: A virtual machine compiling a hot function after it has run many times
Optimizing a call site once the actual type is known

definition: The kernel is the part of the operating system that runs with full access to the hardware. It schedules processes, manages memory, and performs I/O on behalf of programs. User programs ask it to act through system calls instead of touching the hardware themselves.
details: Kernel space is the privileged address region. User space is where ordinary processes run, isolated from the hardware and from each other.
examples: The scheduler deciding which process runs next
The code that implements open, read, and write

definition: KISS, keep it simple, says to prefer the simplest design that meets the need. Extra machinery has to be understood, tested, and changed later. Simplicity is judged by the reader of the code, not by how little time the first version took to type.
examples: A straightforward loop instead of a framework for three items
One code path instead of a configuration matrix nobody uses

definition: Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by considering edges from lightest to heaviest and keeping an edge when its endpoints are not already connected. Union-find answers that connection test. Skipping an edge that would close a cycle is what keeps the result a tree.

complexity.time: O(E log E) to sort the edges, which dominates the nearly constant union-find operations.
complexity.space: O(V) for the union-find structure.

examples: Laying cable by always adding the cheapest link that joins two separate sites

definition: Kubernetes is a system that runs containers across a cluster of machines. You declare the desired state, such as how many copies of a service should run, and it starts, restarts, and places containers to match. It also provides service discovery and load balancing among those copies.
examples: A deployment asking for three replicas
A replacement container started when one stops

definition: A label is the target value paired with an example in supervised learning. The model is trained to predict it. Labels that are wrong or inconsistent become a ceiling on how well the model can do.
prompt: What is a label in supervised learning?
examples: Spam or not spam
The price a house sold for

definition: A large language model is a large neural network, usually a transformer, trained to predict text. Given a prompt, it produces a distribution over the next token and samples or searches from it, repeating to form a reply. Its knowledge is whatever was in the training data and the prompt, and it can state false things fluently.
examples: A model completing a prompt with the next tokens
A chatbot built on a text-prediction model

definition: Leader election chooses one node in a group to coordinate, so the others do not all try to write at once. The leader stays leader until it fails or cannot be reached, and then the remaining nodes elect another. A split view of who is leader is the failure the algorithm has to prevent.
examples: A database primary chosen by the replicas
A Raft term in which one node is leader

definition: Least privilege means granting only the access a task needs, and no more. A service account that only reads one table cannot wipe the database if it is misused. Privileges that are broad 'just in case' become the damage radius of a mistake.
examples: A deploy account that can ship a service and cannot read customer data
A process that can write only its own directory

definition: A lexer reads source characters and groups them into tokens: identifiers, numbers, strings, and operators. It discards insignificant whitespace and comments in most languages. The parser consumes the token stream rather than the raw characters.
examples: Turning a + b into an identifier, a plus, and an identifier
Recognizing a string literal including its quotes

definition: A library is code written to be called by other programs, not to run as a program of its own. It offers functions or types for a particular job. An application imports it or links against it.
prompt: What is a library in programming?
examples: A library of date functions
A compression library called by a server

definition: Linear search checks elements one by one until it finds the target or runs out of elements. The input does not need to be sorted. In the worst case every element is examined.

complexity.time: O(n) in the worst case. O(1) if the target is first.
complexity.space: O(1) extra space.

examples: Finding a name in an unsorted list
Scanning a log for the first error

definition: A linked list stores each element in a node that points at the next node. The list itself holds only the first node, and reaching the element at position k takes k steps. Inserting or removing a node is constant time when you already hold the neighboring node.
details: There is no index access in constant time. Use a list when you splice nodes you already have, not when you need random access.
A singly linked list can only move forward.

complexity.time: Access by position is O(n). Insert or delete at a known node is O(1).
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: A playlist where songs are spliced in without shifting later songs
A free list of reusable blocks inside an allocator

definition: Linux is a kernel, and the usual name for the family of operating systems built around that kernel. It manages processes, memory, files, and devices on servers, phones, and embedded machines. A distribution packages the kernel with user-space tools and a package manager.
examples: A server running a Linux distribution
Containers sharing a Linux kernel with the host

definition: The Liskov substitution principle says a subtype must be usable anywhere the base type is expected, without breaking the caller's assumptions. Overridden methods should not demand more from callers or guarantee less in return. A square type that cannot change width and height independently is the classic violation of a rectangle base.
examples: A read-only file subtype that throws on write, where the base type promised write
A subtype that strengthens a precondition the caller was not required to meet

definition: A load balancer spreads incoming requests across several instances of a service. It sends each request to a healthy instance, using a rule such as round robin or fewest connections. When an instance fails its health check, the balancer stops sending it work.
details: A layer-4 balancer forwards connections using addresses and ports. A layer-7 balancer can look at the HTTP request and route on the path or host.
examples: Several web servers behind one address
Removing an instance that fails its health check

definition: A logarithm says how many times a base must be multiplied by itself to reach a number. In computing the usual base is 2, so log2 of n is how many times n can be cut in half. That count is the cost of binary search and of operations on a balanced tree.
details: Changing the base only multiplies the logarithm by a constant, so it does not change a Big-O class.

definition: Logging records discrete events as timestamped messages, so a later reader can reconstruct what a process did. A log line should say what happened and identify the request, and it should not contain secrets. Volume and retention are part of the design, because logs have a cost.
examples: A line for each failed payment, with an id and a reason
A request id included on every line from that request

definition: A loss function measures how wrong a prediction is compared with the target. Training changes parameters to make the loss smaller. The choice of loss states what kind of mistake the model should care about.
examples: Squared error for a numeric prediction
Cross-entropy for a classification

definition: A MAC address is the link-layer address of a network interface, used to deliver a frame across one local network. It is not used to route a packet across the internet; the IP address is. Switches learn which MAC address sits on which port.
examples: The address of a laptop's network interface
A switch forwarding a frame to the port that last sent that address

definition: Machine code is a program encoded as the bytes the processor executes. Each instruction is a binary pattern defined by the instruction set. It is the usual output of a compiler or an assembler, and it is not meant to be written by hand.
examples: The bytes of a compiled executable
An instruction word the CPU decodes directly

definition: Machine learning builds a model by adjusting its parameters on data, instead of writing the decision rule by hand. The trained model then makes predictions on new inputs. The quality of those predictions depends on the data, the model, and the question being asked.
examples: A spam filter trained on labeled mail
A model that predicts the next word

definition: Maintainability is how easily a system can be understood, fixed, and changed. Clear boundaries, tests, and names are what make a change local and checkable. A system can be correct today and still be hard to maintain.
examples: A module small enough to change with confidence
A test that fails when a later edit breaks a rule

definition: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers, arranged in rows and columns. Matrix multiplication combines linear transformations such as scaling, rotation, and translation. Machine-learning weights and batches of inputs are stored the same way.
prompt: What is a matrix in mathematics?
details: Matrix multiplication is not commutative. The order of transformations matters.

definition: Memoization caches the result of a function under its arguments and returns the cached result on a later call with the same arguments. It turns an exponential recursion with overlapping subproblems into a much smaller number of real calls. It is the top-down form of dynamic programming.
details: It helps only when the same arguments recur. A function whose arguments are almost always new just fills the cache.
The cache key has to include every input the result depends on.

complexity.space: Proportional to the number of distinct argument combinations that are stored.

examples: Caching Fibonacci results so each n is computed once
Caching the best score for each subarray in a recursion

definition: Memory allocation reserves a block of the heap for a new object and returns a pointer to it. The allocator tracks which ranges are free and which are in use. Freeing returns a block to that pool; in a garbage-collected language the collector does the return.
examples: malloc or new returning a block
An allocator splitting a free range to satisfy a request

definition: The memory heap is the region where a process stores dynamically allocated objects. The program asks for a block, an allocator finds space, and the block remains until it is freed or collected. The name has nothing to do with the heap data structure.
prompt: What is the memory heap?
examples: An object created with malloc or new
A buffer whose size is known only at run time

definition: The memory hierarchy is the stack of stores from fastest and smallest to slowest and largest: registers, caches, main memory, then disk. Each level holds copies or overflow from the level above it. Programs run fast when the data they touch stays in a fast level.
examples: Registers, then L1, L2, and L3 cache, then RAM, then SSD
A working set that fits in cache and one that does not

definition: A merge conflict happens when two commits changed the same part of a file and Git cannot combine them automatically. Git marks the conflicting regions and waits for a person to choose the result. Resolving it means editing the file to the intended contents and recording that choice.
examples: Two branches editing the same function
A generated lockfile changed on both sides

definition: Merge sort divides a list in half, sorts each half, and merges the two sorted halves by always taking the smaller front item. The split is the divide step and the merge is the combine step. The usual array version is stable and uses extra space proportional to the input.

complexity.time: O(n log n) in the best, average, and worst cases.
complexity.space: O(n) extra space for the usual array merge.

examples: Sorting a large file that does not fit in one pass of memory
A stable sort of records by a key

definition: A message queue stores messages from producers until consumers take them. It decouples the sender's timing from the receiver's and can absorb a burst. Consumers have to handle duplicates and failures, because a message may be delivered more than once if a consumer crashes after receiving it.
examples: Orders placed on a queue for a worker to fulfill
A buffer between a web request and a slow email sender

definition: A method is a function attached to an object or a class. It usually reads or changes that object through a reference called this or self. The call reads as a request to the object rather than as a free function.
prompt: What is a method in programming?
examples: A list method that appends an item
An account method that applies a payment

definition: Method overloading defines several methods with the same name and different parameters. The language picks which one to call from the arguments at the call site, usually at compile time. It is not the same as overriding, which picks the method from the object's actual type at run time.
examples: A draw method that accepts either a color or a color plus a line width
Several constructors with different parameter lists

definition: Method overriding replaces a method inherited from a parent with a new implementation in the subclass. The signature stays the same, and a call through the parent type runs the subclass method. That is the mechanism behind subtype polymorphism.
details: The subclass method should honor the parent's contract. Doing less, or demanding more from the caller, breaks substitution.
examples: A subclass logging method that writes JSON instead of plain text
A shape's area method replaced in Circle and in Rectangle

definition: Metrics are numeric measurements taken over time, such as a count of requests, a gauge of queue depth, or a histogram of latency. They are aggregated, so they stay cheap at high volume. They show trends and are a weak tool for explaining one individual failure.
examples: A counter of HTTP responses by status code
A histogram of how long queries take

definition: A microservice architecture splits an application into many services, each owning one capability and deployed independently. Teams can release their service without releasing the others. The cost is operational: network calls, partial failure, and data that is no longer in one database.
examples: Separate services for catalog, cart, and payment
A release of one service that does not redeploy the rest

definition: Middleware is code in a request pipeline that runs before or after the main handler. Each layer can read or modify the request or the response, or stop the pipeline. Authentication, logging, and compression are often middleware.
prompt: What is middleware in a web application?
examples: A layer that rejects a request with no session
A layer that logs each request and then calls the next layer

definition: A migration is a versioned change to a database schema, or to data that must move with that change. Migrations are applied in order so every environment can reach the same schema. A migration that rewrites a large table needs a plan that does not stop the application for the whole rewrite.
prompt: What is a database migration?
examples: Adding a column
Backfilling a new column and then enforcing it as not null

definition: A minimum spanning tree is a subset of a connected, weighted, undirected graph that connects every vertex, has no cycles, and has the smallest total edge weight. It has exactly one fewer edge than there are vertices. Kruskal's algorithm and Prim's algorithm both construct one.
examples: Connecting sites with the least total cable
A cheapest set of links that keeps a network connected

definition: A dataset is the collection of examples a model is trained or evaluated on. How it was gathered, and what it leaves out, shows up in the model's behavior. Splitting it into training, validation, and test portions is what makes evaluation honest.
prompt: What is a dataset in machine learning?
examples: A table of labeled emails
A set of images with captions

definition: A model is a parameterized function that maps inputs to a prediction. Training sets the parameters. Two models can share an architecture and differ only in the parameters they learned.
prompt: What is a model in machine learning?
examples: A neural network with a particular set of weights
A linear model with a weight per feature

definition: A mock is a test double that records how it was called and lets the test assert on those calls. It checks the interaction, not only the returned value. Over-specifying calls makes tests break when the collaboration changes in a way the behavior did not.
examples: Asserting that a notifier was called once with a given message
A mock repository that expects a save

definition: Model evaluation measures how well a model does on a task, using data or criteria that were not used to fit it. A single accuracy number can hide failures on a slice of the inputs that matters. The metric has to match the decision the model will actually support.
examples: Accuracy on a held-out test set
An error rate broken down by a group the product cares about

definition: A parameter is a number inside a model that training adjusts, such as a weight in a network. The set of parameters is what distinguishes a trained model from the architecture alone. At inference the parameters stay fixed.
prompt: What is a parameter in a machine learning model?
examples: A weight on a connection in a network
The coefficients of a linear model

definition: Modularity is dividing a system into parts with clear boundaries, so each part can be understood and changed with limited knowledge of the others. A module hides its internals and publishes an interface. The boundaries are what make independent change possible.
examples: A billing module that other code reaches only through its API
A parser separated from the code that uses the parsed tree

definition: A module is a unit of code with its own scope. It exports some names and hides the rest, and it is usually a file or a small group of files. Other code uses it only through the names it exports.
prompt: What is a module in programming?
examples: A file that exports a date parser and hides its helpers
A math module that exports only its public functions

definition: The modulo operation returns the remainder after division. Programs use it to wrap a number into a fixed range, such as a circular buffer or a hash bucket. Languages disagree on the sign of the remainder when the dividend is negative.
examples: Turning any integer into an index inside a fixed array
Alternating between two choices with remainder 2

definition: A monitor is a concurrency construct that combines mutual exclusion with the ability to wait for a condition. Only one thread runs inside the monitor at a time, and a thread can wait until another thread signals that the condition holds. It is a higher-level pattern than a bare mutex.
prompt: What is a monitor in concurrent programming?
examples: A bounded buffer where producers wait for space and consumers wait for an item
A lock plus a condition variable around a queue

definition: Monitoring collects signals from a running system and checks them against conditions you defined in advance. Dashboards and alerts are how people see the result. It answers known questions, such as whether error rate or latency has crossed a line.
examples: A chart of request latency
An alert when the error rate exceeds a threshold

definition: A monolith is an application built and deployed as one unit. Calls between its parts are in-process, and its data often lives in one database. It is simpler to operate than many services, until the codebase or the scaling needs push toward a split.
examples: One web application that handles pages, API, and jobs
One deployable artifact for the whole product

definition: Multi-factor authentication requires evidence from more than one category: something the person knows, something they have, or something they are. A password plus a code from a device is the common case of two factors. Stealing the password alone is then not enough to sign in.
examples: A password plus a code from an authenticator
A password plus a hardware security key

definition: A mutex is a lock that only one thread may hold at a time. A thread that locks it excludes the others from the protected section until it unlocks. The mutex is owned by the thread that locked it, which is the usual difference from a binary semaphore.
examples: Protecting a shared counter
Guarding a list that several threads push onto

definition: NAT rewrites packet addresses so several machines on a private network can share one public address. The router tracks each flow and translates between the private address and the public one. Inbound connections are not reachable unless a mapping was created for them.
examples: A home router sharing one public address
A connection from a private host appearing to come from the router

definition: A computer network is a set of machines that can exchange data over links. Addressing says which machine a message is for, and forwarding moves the message toward that machine. The internet is many networks connected together.
examples: A home network of phones and a laptop
A data-center network between servers

definition: A switch forwards frames inside one local network, using MAC addresses to choose the outgoing port. It learns which address is behind which port by watching traffic. Unlike a router, it does not route packets between IP networks.
prompt: What is a network switch?
examples: An office switch connecting many computers on one LAN
A frame delivered only to the port that leads to its destination

definition: A neural network is a stack of layers that transform an input, each layer a weighted sum followed by a nonlinear activation. Training sets the weights by gradient descent. Without the nonlinearities, stacking layers would collapse into one linear transform.
examples: A network that classifies images
A network that maps text tokens to a next-token distribution

definition: Normalization organizes a relational schema so each fact is stored once, by splitting data into tables related by keys. Higher normal forms remove particular kinds of redundancy and the update anomalies that come with it. The usual stopping point for transactional schemas is third normal form or Boyce-Codd normal form.
prompt: What is normalization in a relational database?
details: This is not feature scaling in machine learning, which is also called normalization.
First normal form requires atomic column values. Later forms remove dependencies that are not on the key.
examples: Moving a customer's address out of every order row into a customer table
A schema in which changing a product name updates one row

definition: NoSQL is a loose name for databases that are not the relational model: documents, key-value pairs, wide columns, or graphs. They usually trade some of the relational guarantees or query flexibility for a particular access pattern or for easier horizontal scaling. It is a family of models, not one product.
examples: A document store of JSON objects
A key-value store used as a cache or a session store
A graph store of people and relationships

definition: Null is a value that means there is no object, or no result, where a reference would otherwise be. Reading fields through null is an error in most languages. Some languages use a type that explicitly includes absence, so the missing value is visible to the type checker.
examples: A search that finds no match
An optional profile field the user left empty

definition: An object is a value that bundles state with the operations that use that state. It has an identity, so two objects can carry the same data and still be different objects. In class-based languages, an object is created from a class.
prompt: What is an object in object-oriented programming?
examples: One particular user, distinct from another user with the same name
A window on screen with its own position and size

definition: Observability is how well you can understand a system's internal state from the signals it emits. Logs, metrics, and traces are the usual signals. Monitoring checks conditions you already thought of; observability is what lets you ask a new question during an incident.
examples: Tracing one slow request across several services
Breaking down an error rate by endpoint and by version

definition: The open-closed principle says a unit should be open to extension and closed to modification. New behavior is added by new code, such as a new implementation of an interface, rather than by editing a unit that callers already depend on. Some changes still have to modify existing code; the principle says which way to prefer.
examples: Adding a new exporter by implementing an Exporter interface
A pricing rule added as a new strategy object

definition: An operating system manages hardware and provides the services programs run on: processes, memory, files, and devices. The kernel is the privileged core. The rest of the system, such as shells and libraries, sits on top of it.
examples: A desktop system running many applications at once
A server system scheduling processes and serving files

definition: An ORM maps rows to objects and lets application code read and write those objects instead of writing every SQL statement by hand. The mapping is convenient and can hide the queries it generates. Knowing the generated SQL still matters, because the cost is the database's cost, not the object's.
examples: Loading a user object that came from the users table
A save that becomes an insert or an update

definition: Overfitting is when a model fits the training data, including its noise, and does worse on new data. The training loss keeps falling while the validation loss rises. A simpler model, more data, or regularization are the usual responses.
examples: A model that memorizes training rows and misses on the test set
A widening gap between training accuracy and validation accuracy

definition: A package is a versioned bundle of code that a project can depend on. It usually contains modules plus metadata such as a name and a version. A package manager downloads it and records the dependency.
prompt: What is a package in programming?
examples: A released library pinned to version 2.1.0
A package manifest listing dependencies

definition: A packet is a chunk of data carried at the network layer, with a header that includes source and destination addresses. The payload is the data being sent. Packets are routed independently, and a message larger than the path allows is split into several of them.
examples: An IP packet carrying part of a download
A header with a destination IP address

definition: A page is a fixed-size block of virtual memory, and the unit the operating system maps onto physical frames. Common sizes are 4 KiB and larger huge pages. The page table records where each virtual page currently lives.
prompt: What is a page in virtual memory?
examples: A 4 KiB block mapped to a physical frame
A page marked not present, so the next access faults

definition: A page fault is the exception raised when a process touches a virtual page that is not currently mapped for that access. A valid fault loads the page from disk or allocates a frame and then resumes the process. An invalid fault, such as a bad address, is delivered to the process as an error.
examples: The first write to a freshly allocated page
A touch of an unmapped address that becomes a segmentation fault

definition: Parallelism is actually executing several operations at the same time, on multiple processors or cores. It is a way to finish a divisible amount of work sooner. A concurrent design can run on one processor; a parallel execution cannot.
examples: Four cores each sorting a quarter of an array
A GPU applying one operation to many pixels at once

definition: A parameter is a name in a function definition for a value the caller supplies. Inside the function it behaves like a local variable whose starting value came from the call. The parameter is the slot; the argument is what is placed in the slot.
examples: The width and height of a function that computes an area
An optional parameter with a default

definition: A parser reads tokens and builds a tree that reflects the grammar of the language. It is where operator precedence and nesting are decided. A syntax error is the parser rejecting a token sequence the grammar does not allow.
examples: Building a tree in which multiplication sits below addition
Rejecting a missing closing parenthesis

definition: Partitioning splits one logical table into smaller physical parts, often by a range or a hash of a column. The parts may live on one machine. Queries that match the partition key can skip the other parts; the table still looks like one table to many queries.
prompt: What is partitioning in a database?
details: Sharding is partitioning spread across nodes so the data no longer fits one machine. Partitioning on one machine is often about manageability and pruning.
examples: A logs table partitioned by month
Dropping an old month by dropping one partition

definition: Password hashing stores a slow, salted hash of a password instead of the password. A slow function, such as Argon2, bcrypt, or scrypt, makes guessing expensive. A fast hash such as plain SHA-256 is the wrong tool, because guesses can be checked too quickly.
details: The salt is stored beside the hash. Verification hashes the submitted password with the same salt and compares the results.
examples: A user table that stores a hash and a salt, not a password
Argon2 as the hashing function

definition: Path traversal happens when a file path is built from untrusted text and that text contains parent-directory segments. The risk is reading or writing a file outside the directory the program intended. The defense is to resolve the path and reject it unless it stays inside the allowed directory.
examples: A download handler that confines paths to one folder
Rejecting a resolved path that escapes the base directory

definition: A pipe is a one-way byte stream between processes. One end writes and the other reads, and the kernel buffers the bytes in between. A shell pipeline connects the output of one program to the input of the next with pipes.
prompt: What is a pipe between processes?
examples: The connection inside ls | grep
A parent reading the standard output of a child

definition: A pixel is one sample of a picture, a single point in the grid that makes up an image, holding a color. The image's width and height are counts of pixels. A pixel is not a physical dot on every display, which may light several hardware elements to show one pixel.
examples: A 1920 by 1080 image, which has that many pixels
One pixel storing red, green, and blue values

definition: A pointer is a value that stores the address of something in memory. Following it yields the bytes stored at that address. Pointers make sharing and dynamic structures possible, and they fail when the address is wrong or the target is already gone.
details: A null pointer does not point at an object. Using it is an error.
A dangling pointer refers to memory that has already been freed.
examples: The address of the first element of an array
A link from one list node to the next

definition: Polymorphism lets one call run different implementations depending on the actual object. The caller programs against a shared type, such as a parent class or an interface, and each subtype supplies its own method. The caller does not need a branch for every subtype.
examples: A draw call that paints a circle or a rectangle depending on the shape
A log call that writes to a file or to the network through the same interface

definition: A port is a number that selects which application on a host a TCP or UDP packet belongs to. The host is selected by the IP address; the port selects the socket on that host. Well-known ports are conventions, such as 443 for HTTPS, not a property of the protocol.
prompt: What is a network port?
examples: Port 443 for HTTPS
Two services on one machine, distinguished by port

definition: A prefix sum array stores the sum of every element up to each index. After that array is built, the sum of any contiguous range is the difference of two prefix values. Building it is linear, and each later range query is constant time.
details: With prefix[0] = 0 and prefix[i] equal to the sum of the first i elements, the sum from index l through r is prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l].

complexity.time: O(n) to build. O(1) per range sum afterward.
complexity.space: O(n) for the prefix array.

examples: Many range-sum queries on an array that does not change
Counting how many items fall in a score band

definition: Prim's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by growing one connected component. It repeatedly adds the lightest edge that leaves the component and reaches a new vertex, using a priority queue to find that edge. The result is a tree because each added edge reaches a vertex not yet included.

complexity.time: O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.
complexity.space: O(V) for the queue and the visited set.

examples: Growing a network outward from a starting site, always by the cheapest new link

definition: A primary key is the column or columns that uniquely identify each row of a table. The database rejects a second row with the same key, and it rejects null in the key. Other tables refer to that identity with foreign keys.
examples: A numeric user id
A composite key of order id plus line number

definition: A primitive type is a basic type built into the language, such as an integer, a floating-point number, a boolean, or a character. Its values are usually stored directly, rather than as a pointer to a separate object. Which types count as primitive depends on the language.
examples: A 64-bit integer
A boolean true or false

definition: A priority queue is a collection that removes the element with the highest priority, rather than the oldest or the newest. Insert and remove-highest are the operations. A binary heap is the usual implementation.

complexity.time: With a binary heap, insert and remove-highest are O(log n). Peek is O(1).
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: Tasks served by urgency instead of arrival time
The frontier of Dijkstra's algorithm

definition: A private key is the half of a key pair that must stay secret. It decrypts what the public key encrypted and it creates signatures. Anyone who obtains it can impersonate the owner, so storage and access to it are the sensitive part of the pair.
examples: A key kept on a server and used to sign tokens
A key that decrypts a message encrypted to its public pair

definition: A process is a running program with its own address space, open files, and at least one thread of execution. The operating system isolates processes from each other. Creating a process copies or builds that environment; ending it releases it.
details: A process is the isolation boundary. Threads inside one process share its memory.
examples: A web server process and a database process on the same machine
A shell starting a command as a child process

definition: A promise stands for a value that is not available yet. It later becomes fulfilled with a value or rejected with a failure, and other code can attach work to run at that moment. Some languages call the same idea a future, and a few split the producer side from a read-only handle.
details: A promise settles once. Attaching a callback after it has settled still runs the callback with the stored result.
examples: The result of an HTTP request that has not finished
A file read that will either return bytes or fail

definition: A prompt is the input text given to a language model to steer what it produces. Instructions, examples, and the user's question are all part of the prompt. Changing the prompt changes the output without changing the model's parameters.
prompt: What is a prompt for a language model?
examples: An instruction followed by a question
A few examples of the desired format, then a new case

definition: Property-based testing generates many inputs and checks a property that should hold for all of them, instead of listing individual examples. When an input fails, the tool tries to shrink it to a smaller failing case. The property is the specification; the examples are produced by the tool.
examples: Encoding and then decoding yields the original value
Sorting a list produces a list of the same length

definition: A proxy is an intermediary that makes a request on a client's behalf. The client talks to the proxy, and the proxy talks to the origin server. Proxies are used for caching, filtering, and hiding the client's address from the origin.
examples: A corporate proxy that clients must use to reach the web
A caching proxy in front of a slow origin

definition: A public key is the half of a key pair that may be shared. Others use it to encrypt to the owner or to verify the owner's signatures. It does not have to be kept secret, and it cannot by itself decrypt or sign.
examples: A key published in a certificate
A key used to verify a software signature

definition: Public-key infrastructure is the system of certificates, issuers, and trust decisions that lets parties who have never met rely on each other's public keys. Certificate authorities sign certificates, and verifiers keep a set of root authorities they trust. A chain of signatures from a root down to the server's certificate is what a browser checks.
examples: A browser trusting a site because a known authority signed its certificate
An internal authority that issues certificates to services

definition: Publish-subscribe delivers each published message to every subscriber of a topic, and the publisher does not name the subscribers. Adding a subscriber does not require changing the publisher. Delivery is usually asynchronous, and ordering guarantees depend on the system.
examples: An order-placed event read by billing and by shipping
A topic that any number of workers can subscribe to

definition: A pull request is a proposal to merge one branch into another, together with a place to discuss and review the change. The name is common on GitHub; other hosts call the same idea a merge request. Merging the request creates the merge, or fast-forwards the target branch.
examples: A review of a feature branch before it reaches main
A discussion attached to a proposed fix

definition: A query is a request to a database to read or change data. A read query describes the rows to return. A write query inserts, updates, or deletes rows. The text of the query is not the same thing as the plan the engine uses to run it.
prompt: What is a database query?
examples: A select that returns open orders
An update that marks an order paid

definition: The query planner chooses how to execute a query: which indexes to use, in what order to join tables, and how to access each one. It estimates costs from statistics about the data. A bad estimate can pick a slow plan even though a fast one exists.
examples: Choosing an index lookup instead of a full scan
Choosing a join order for three tables

definition: A queue is a collection that removes the element that has been waiting the longest. Enqueue adds at the back and dequeue removes from the front, both in constant time when implemented with a linked list or a circular buffer. It models work served in arrival order.

complexity.time: Enqueue and dequeue are O(1).
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: Print jobs served in the order they were submitted
The frontier of a breadth-first search

definition: QUIC is a transport protocol that runs over UDP and provides reliable streams plus encryption in the protocol itself. Several streams share one connection, so a loss on one stream does not stall the others the way TCP head-of-line blocking does. HTTP/3 uses QUIC.
examples: HTTP/3 connections
A multiplexed connection that keeps moving when one stream loses a packet

definition: Quick sort picks a pivot, partitions the other elements into those less than the pivot and those greater, and sorts the two sides. Average cost is n log n when pivots split the input reasonably evenly. A pivot that is always the extreme element degrades the sort to quadratic time.
details: The typical in-place version is not stable.
Choosing the pivot at random, or as the median of a few samples, makes the bad split unlikely.

complexity.time: Average O(n log n). Worst case O(n^2).
complexity.space: O(log n) average stack space for the recursive form, O(n) in the worst case.

examples: The default sort in several standard libraries
Sorting numbers in memory where extra allocation should stay small

definition: A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the uncontrolled timing of concurrent operations. The program is correct for some interleavings and wrong for others. Synchronization, or avoiding the shared mutable state, removes the race.
examples: Two threads incrementing a shared counter and losing an update
Checking a file exists and then opening it, after another process deleted it

definition: Radix sort orders integers or fixed-length strings one digit position at a time, using a stable sort such as counting sort for each position. Starting from the least significant digit produces a correct order of the whole key. It is not a comparison sort, and it needs keys that split into digits.

complexity.time: O(d * (n + k)), where d is the number of digits and k is the digit alphabet size.
complexity.space: O(n + k) for the stable digit sort.

examples: Sorting fixed-length identifiers
Sorting 32-bit integers four bits at a time

definition: RAM is the main working memory of the computer, larger and slower than a cache and much faster than disk. It holds the code and data of running programs. It is volatile: its contents are lost when power goes away.
examples: The memory an operating system assigns to a process
A dataset loaded into memory so later reads do not touch disk

definition: Rasterization turns geometric shapes, usually triangles, into the pixels they cover. For each pixel it decides which triangle is in front and what color to write. It is the approach real-time graphics uses, as opposed to casting rays from the camera.
examples: A triangle drawn into a frame buffer
A depth test that keeps the closest surface

definition: Rate limiting caps how often a client may call a service in a window of time. Excess requests are rejected or delayed. It protects capacity and limits the damage of a buggy or abusive client.
examples: An API that allows one hundred requests per minute per key
A login endpoint that slows repeated attempts

definition: A rebase replays a series of commits onto a new base, creating new commits with new hashes. The branch then looks as if it was started from that new base. Rewriting commits that other people already have forces them to reconcile the rewritten history.
prompt: What does git rebase do?
details: Rebase rewrites history. Do not rebase commits that have been shared, unless everyone using them expects the rewrite.
examples: Replaying a feature branch onto the latest main
Squashing several local commits before they are shared

definition: Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller input. A base case must stop the calls, or they continue until the call stack runs out. Each call has its own parameters and local variables.
details: The depth of recursion is limited by the call stack. A deep recursion can be rewritten as a loop with an explicit stack.
examples: Walking a directory tree
Computing a factorial from the factorial of a smaller number

definition: A red-black tree is a binary search tree whose nodes are colored so the tree stays approximately balanced. No red node has a red child, and every path from the root to a leaf has the same number of black nodes. The longest path is at most twice the shortest, so operations stay logarithmic, with fewer rotations on insert than an AVL tree.

complexity.time: Search, insert, and delete are O(log n) in the worst case.
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: The ordered map in several standard libraries
A scheduler's ordered set of timers

definition: Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing its observable behavior. The point is to make a later change easier or to make the code clearer. Tests that already describe the behavior are what make the rewrite safe.
examples: Extracting a function from a long method
Renaming a misleading variable and updating every use

definition: A reference type is a type whose variable holds a reference to a value stored elsewhere, not the value's own bytes. Two variables can refer to the same object, so a change through one is visible through the other. Objects and arrays are reference types in many languages.
details: Assigning a reference copies the reference, not the object. A later mutation is shared; a later reassignment of one variable is not.
examples: Two variables pointing at the same list
Passing an object into a function that mutates it

definition: A register is a small, very fast storage slot inside the CPU. Instructions operate on registers and move data between registers and memory. There are few of them, and the compiler or the assembly programmer decides what lives there.
prompt: What is a CPU register?
examples: A register holding the current loop index
The stack pointer register

definition: A regression test checks that a behavior which used to work still works, especially a bug that was fixed. It stays in the suite so the same defect is not reintroduced. Any test can serve this role once it pins down a behavior.
examples: A test added with a bug fix
A suite run before every release

definition: Regularization discourages a model from fitting the training data too closely. A penalty on large weights, dropout, or early stopping are common forms. It trades a bit of training fit for better behavior on new data.
examples: A penalty added for large weights
Stopping training when validation loss stops improving

definition: Reinforcement learning trains a policy by trying actions and observing rewards, not by showing it the correct action. The learner has to balance trying new actions against repeating actions that have paid off. It fits settings where the quality of a sequence of actions is known, even when the best next step is not labeled.
examples: A game-playing agent rewarded for winning
A controller rewarded for staying upright

definition: A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns, related by keys. Queries say what to retrieve, and the engine decides how. Constraints such as keys and uniqueness are enforced by the database rather than only by application code.
examples: Orders in one table and customers in another, joined by a customer id
A unique constraint on an email column

definition: Reliability is the likelihood that a system does what it is supposed to do, correctly, for a period of time. A system can be up and still unreliable if its answers are wrong. Measuring it means defining the failure, not only the uptime.
examples: A payment call that either charges once or fails cleanly
A storage system that does not lose an acknowledged write

definition: Rendering turns a description of a scene into an image. The description names geometry, materials, lights, and a camera; the image is the grid of colors a viewer sees. Real-time rendering keeps up with interaction, and offline rendering spends longer for a single picture.
prompt: What is rendering in computer graphics?
examples: A game drawing a frame
A ray tracer producing one image of a scene

definition: Replication keeps copies of the same data on more than one node. It is used for failover and to spread reads. The copies can lag, so a read of a replica may not yet show the latest write, depending on the consistency the system provides.
examples: A primary database with replicas that take over if it fails
Read queries sent to a replica

definition: A repository is the stored project: its files, its commits, and the references such as branches and tags. In Git it can be a working copy plus the history, or a bare copy that has only the history. Cloning copies that history to another place.
prompt: What is a version-control repository?
examples: A project's .git directory and working tree
A bare repository on a server that people push to

definition: Requirements are the statements of what the software must do and which constraints it must meet. They describe the need, from the point of view of the people who will use or operate the system. They are the input to design, and they are what acceptance is judged against.
examples: A user must be able to reset a password
The service must answer within a stated time

definition: Resolution is the number of pixels in each dimension of an image or a display. A higher resolution can show finer detail and costs more memory and more work to render. It is a count of samples, not a physical size, unless a pixel density is also given.
examples: A render target smaller than the window, scaled up

definition: REST is an architectural style for APIs built around resources, identified by URLs, manipulated with a small set of methods, and transferred in representations such as JSON. Interactions are stateless: each request carries what the server needs. Many APIs called REST are JSON over HTTP and do not follow every constraint of the style.
details: The style also calls for cacheable responses and a uniform interface. Using HTTP and JSON does not by itself meet those constraints.
examples: GET /orders/42 returning one order
DELETE /orders/42 removing that order

definition: Retrieval-augmented generation fetches documents relevant to a query and includes them in the model's prompt before it answers. The model can then use facts it was not trained on, or that would not fit in its weights. The answer is only as current and as relevant as the documents that were retrieved.
examples: A question answered from a company's internal documents
A search step followed by a prompt that quotes the passages found

definition: A retry repeats a request that failed because of a transient error, such as a timeout or an unavailable host. It helps only when the operation is safe to repeat, or when an idempotency key makes it so. Retrying a permanent error, or retrying immediately in a tight loop, makes an outage worse.
examples: Repeating a timed-out read
Giving up after a few attempts and returning an error

definition: A return value is the result a function hands back to its caller. The call itself takes on that value, so the caller can store it or pass it on. A function can also return nothing and be called only for its effect.
examples: A function returning a computed total
A function whose only job is to write a file

definition: A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and accepts incoming requests for them. Clients connect to the proxy, which forwards each request to a server behind it. It is where TLS is often terminated and where requests are routed or load balanced.
examples: A proxy that terminates TLS and forwards plain requests to application processes
A single public address in front of several services

definition: RGB represents a color as three intensities: red, green, and blue. Each channel is a number, often from 0 to 255 in an 8-bit image, or a floating-point value in a renderer. Adding light works in RGB; mixing paint does not follow the same arithmetic.
examples: White as full red, green, and blue
A pixel stored as three bytes

definition: Risk combines how likely a harmful event is with how bad it would be. A severe weakness that is unreachable may be a lower risk than a modest weakness on a public endpoint. Prioritizing work means comparing risks, not only listing weaknesses.
prompt: What is risk in security?
examples: A public endpoint with a known weakness
A severe bug on a system that is not connected

definition: A router forwards IP packets between networks. It chooses the next hop from a routing table and sends the packet out the corresponding interface. It operates on packets and IP addresses, not on a single local link's frames.
examples: The gateway between a home network and an internet provider
A router choosing the next hop toward a destination prefix

definition: A row is one record in a table, a single tuple of values, one for each column. It is the unit that a primary key identifies. Two rows can hold the same values only if the table's constraints allow it.
prompt: What is a row in a relational database?
examples: One user
One line item of an order

definition: RPC, remote procedure call, invokes a procedure on another machine as if it were a local call. The arguments are sent over the network and the result comes back. The call can fail because of the network even when the procedure itself is correct, which a local call would not do.
examples: A generated client that calls a named method on a service
A request that names a procedure and its arguments

definition: The runtime is the support code that a program needs while it is executing: memory allocation, garbage collection, scheduling of tasks, and the standard library's ties to the operating system. Compiled machine code still has a runtime. It is not the same thing as the compiler, which has already finished.
examples: A garbage collector running during a program
The scheduler behind async tasks

definition: A salt is a random value stored with a password hash and mixed into the hash. Identical passwords then produce different hashes, and a precomputed table of hashes does not apply to every user. The salt is not a secret; it exists to make each hash unique.
examples: A different random salt for each user
A hash that cannot be matched against a single precomputed table

definition: Sandboxing runs code with a restricted set of privileges, so a mistake or a hostile input is confined. The sandbox decides which files, network calls, and system calls are allowed. It is the containment used for untrusted documents, plugins, and multi-tenant workloads.
examples: A browser renderer process with limited system access
A build job that cannot reach the production network

definition: Scalability is the ability to handle more load by adding resources, without a redesign. Vertical scaling adds capacity to one machine. Horizontal scaling adds more machines, which only works if the work can be split.
examples: Adding application instances behind a load balancer
Moving a larger working set onto a machine with more memory

definition: Scheduling is how the operating system chooses which runnable thread runs on a processor, and for how long. Preemptive scheduling can interrupt a running thread. Cooperative scheduling waits for the thread to give up the processor itself.
examples: A time slice that expires and lets another thread run
A priority scheduler that runs a high-priority thread first

definition: A schema is the structure of the data: the tables, columns, types, and constraints. It is separate from the rows stored in that structure. Changing the schema is a migration, not an ordinary write.
prompt: What is a database schema?
examples: The definition of the users table
A constraint that email values are unique

definition: Scope is the region of a program where a name is visible. With lexical scope, the usual rule, a name is visible in the block where it is declared and in blocks nested inside that one. Code outside that region cannot use the name.
prompt: What is scope in a program?
details: An inner binding can shadow an outer one of the same name. Inside the inner block, the outer name is hidden.
examples: A loop variable that exists only inside the loop
A function parameter that is invisible to other functions

definition: An SDK is a kit for building software on a platform: libraries, tools, and documentation shipped together. It is aimed at developers, not at the end users of the platform. The application calls the libraries the kit contains.
examples: A mobile platform kit with libraries and a simulator
A kit for calling a vendor's HTTP API

definition: Secrets management keeps credentials and keys out of source code and out of images, and provides them to a running process through a controlled channel. Secrets are rotated, and access to them is limited to the workload that needs them. A secret committed to a repository has to be considered exposed.
examples: A database password injected at deploy time
A key read from a secrets store rather than from the repository

definition: Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and swaps it into the next output position. It does about n-squared comparisons regardless of the input order. The usual in-place version is not stable, because a swap can move an equal element past another.

complexity.time: O(n^2) in the best, average, and worst cases.
complexity.space: O(1) extra space.

examples: A teaching sort that makes the 'pick the next minimum' step obvious

definition: Semantic analysis checks the meaning of a program after it has parsed: that names refer to something, that types line up, and that the rules beyond the grammar hold. A program can be syntactically valid and still fail here. The result is often an annotated tree the code generator can trust.
examples: Rejecting the use of a variable that was never declared
Checking that the branches of a conditional return the same type

definition: Semantic versioning numbers releases as major.minor.patch. The patch number changes for compatible fixes, the minor number for compatible additions, and the major number when existing callers must change. The scheme only works if the project actually treats those categories honestly.
examples: 1.2.3 to 1.2.4 for a bug fix
1.4.0 to 2.0.0 when an existing function is removed

definition: A semaphore is a counter that threads wait on and signal. Wait decrements the counter, blocking when it would go below zero; signal increments it and wakes a waiter. A counting semaphore allows a fixed number of threads into a section, not only one.
details: A binary semaphore looks like a mutex but has no owner. Any thread may signal it, which is also why it is easier to misuse.
examples: Limiting a pool to ten concurrent users
Signaling that an item has been added to a queue

definition: Separation of concerns puts different responsibilities in different parts of the system. Presentation, business rules, and storage are the usual split. Each part can change for its own reasons without taking on the others' details.
examples: A template that renders HTML and a separate function that computes the numbers
Validation kept out of the database driver

definition: Serialization turns an in-memory value into bytes or text that can be stored or sent. Deserialization rebuilds a value from that representation. Both sides must share a format, or the rebuilt value will be wrong or rejected.
details: Untrusted serialized data should be treated as input, not as a trusted object graph. Rebuilding arbitrary objects from it is a common source of bugs.
examples: Encoding an order as JSON to send to another service
Writing a struct to a file and reading it back

definition: A server is a program that waits for requests and responds to them. It typically holds data or performs an action on behalf of many clients. The same machine can run several servers, distinguished by port or by host name.
examples: A web server answering HTTP
A database server answering queries

definition: Server-side rendering builds the HTML for a page on the server for each request, and sends that HTML to the browser. The user sees content without waiting for client-side code to assemble it. The server does the work on every request, unless a cache stores the result.
examples: A page whose HTML already contains the article text
A server rendering a template with the user's data

definition: Server-side request forgery happens when a server fetches a URL that an outsider supplied. The risk is the server reaching an internal system the outsider could not call directly. The defense is to allow only expected destinations and to refuse addresses that are internal or link-local.
examples: A webhook URL checked against an allowlist
A fetcher that will not call internal addresses

definition: A service is a program that performs one job and is reached over the network through an API. Other software depends on that API rather than on the service's code. It can be deployed and scaled on its own schedule when it is a separate process.
prompt: What is a service in a distributed system?
examples: An authentication service
A billing service called by the order flow

definition: A session is server-side state that remembers an authenticated user across many requests. The browser typically holds only an identifier, often in a cookie, and sends it back so the server can find that state. Ending the session on the server removes the authority, even if the identifier is still sitting in the browser.
examples: A login that creates a session and sets a cookie
A logout that deletes the session

definition: A set is a collection of distinct elements, with no positions and no duplicates. The operations that matter are adding, removing, and testing membership. A hash table or a balanced tree is the usual implementation.
details: Putting an element in twice leaves one copy. Order of iteration is not part of the idea, though a particular implementation may define one.

complexity.time: Membership is O(1) average with hashing, or O(log n) in a balanced tree.
complexity.space: O(n) space for the elements themselves.

examples: The set of user ids already processed
The letters that appear in a word, each once

definition: A shader is a program that runs on the GPU as part of drawing. A vertex shader transforms each vertex, and a fragment shader computes the color of a pixel-sized piece of a surface. Shaders are where lighting and materials are calculated.
examples: A fragment shader that samples a texture
A vertex shader that applies a camera transform

definition: Sharding splits a dataset across nodes by a key, so each node holds a subset of the rows. It scales writes and storage past one machine. A query that does not include the shard key may have to visit every shard, and re-sharding moves data.
examples: Users divided by user id across ten databases
A query for one user that hits only that user's shard

definition: A shell is a program that reads commands and runs them, connecting programs with pipes and redirecting their input and output. It is both an interactive prompt and a language for scripts. A script's behavior depends on the shell it is written for.
examples: An interactive prompt on a server
A script that loops over files and runs a command on each

definition: A shortest-path problem asks for a path between vertices whose total edge weight is as small as possible. On an unweighted graph, fewest edges is the same question, and breadth-first search answers it. Weighted graphs need an algorithm that accounts for the weights, and negative weights rule some of those algorithms out.
examples: The fastest route across a road network
The minimum delay through a series of network links

definition: A signal is a short asynchronous notification delivered to a process, such as a request to terminate or a notice that a child has exited. The process can catch some signals and run a handler, and it cannot catch others. A signal is not a message with a payload of application data.
prompt: What is a signal to a process?
examples: SIGTERM asking a process to shut down
SIGINT from a terminal interrupt

definition: SIMD applies one instruction to several data elements at the same time. A single add can add four pairs of numbers packed in wide registers. It speeds data-parallel loops and does nothing for control-heavy code.
examples: Adding several audio samples with one instruction
A compiler vectorizing a numeric loop

definition: The single responsibility principle says a module should have one reason to change. The reason is a single kind of stakeholder or concern, not a single method. Mixing unrelated reasons in one module means a change for one concern risks the other.
examples: A class that both calculates pay and writes the payroll file, split into two
A module that formats a report and does not also fetch the data

definition: A sliding window keeps a contiguous segment of a sequence and updates the answer as the segment moves, instead of recomputing it from scratch. Growing or shrinking the ends by one element updates a running aggregate. Many substring and subarray problems that look quadratic become linear this way.

complexity.time: Often O(n), when each index enters and leaves the window at most once.
complexity.space: Often O(1) or O(k) for the state inside the window.

examples: The maximum sum of any subarray of length k
The longest substring with no repeated character

definition: A smoke test is a shallow check that a build is alive enough to test further. It does not try to cover behavior in depth. A failed smoke test means stop and look, because the basics are already broken.
examples: A process that starts and answers a health check
A script that signs in and loads the home view

definition: A socket is an endpoint of network communication, identified by a protocol and, for TCP and UDP, by an IP address and a port. A program sends and receives through the socket the operating system gave it. A TCP connection is a pair of sockets.
examples: A server socket waiting for connections on port 443
A client socket connected to a remote address and port

definition: Software architecture is the set of structural decisions that are expensive to change: the major parts, their responsibilities, and how they communicate. It is chosen so the system can meet its quality needs, such as change, scale, and failure. Later design fills in the parts the architecture only outlines.
prompt: What is software architecture?
examples: A decision to split the system into independently deployed services
A decision that all clients talk to one API gateway

definition: Software design is how a component is shaped: its types, its interfaces, and how its responsibilities are divided. It sits under the architecture and is easier to revise than the system's overall structure. Good design makes a change local.
prompt: What is software design?
examples: The types inside one service and how they call each other
The choice of a strategy object for a pricing rule

definition: The software development lifecycle is the path a system takes from a need, through design, building, testing, and release, and on into maintenance. Different processes order those activities differently: a single pass, or many short iterations. The lifecycle is the set of activities, not one particular process diagram.
examples: An iteration that ships a small change from requirement to release
A maintenance release that fixes a defect in a system already in use

definition: SOLID is five design principles for classes and modules: single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, and dependency inversion. Together they push designs toward small units that depend on stable abstractions. They are guidelines, not rules that every change must satisfy mechanically.
examples: A review comment that cites one of the five by name
A module split because it had two unrelated reasons to change

definition: A sort is stable when items that compare equal keep the order they had in the input. That matters when a later sort should break ties using an earlier key. An unstable sort may swap equal items.
examples: Sorting people by city after sorting them by name, and keeping names in order within a city
A UI that sorts by a column without scrambling equal rows

definition: A specification is a precise description of what will be built, detailed enough to design and test against. It turns a requirement into an agreed behavior, including edge cases. It is more exact than the original need and less concerned with how the code is structured.
prompt: What is a specification in software engineering?
examples: An API specification that lists each request and response
A statement of the rounding rule for a money calculation

definition: SQL is the language used to define, query, and change data in a relational database. A query describes the result, and the engine chooses a plan. Dialects differ, but the core of tables, filters, joins, and aggregates is shared.
examples: A select with a where clause
An insert of one row
An update that changes every row matching a condition

definition: SQL injection happens when untrusted text is concatenated into a query and changes the query's structure. The risk is reading or changing data the caller should not reach. The defense is to keep the statement fixed and send values as parameters, so they cannot change the statement.
examples: A query written with placeholders and bound values
An API that never builds SQL by gluing input into the statement

definition: A stack is a collection that removes the element added most recently. Push adds to the top and pop removes from the top, both in constant time. It models nested work that must be finished in the reverse of the order it was started.
